## 3 Architectures

Report issue for preceding element

As large language models can excel in English, their performance varies though across the other languages.
Accordingly, there is a growing need to advance multilingual large language models in order to ensure a balanced performance across a broader range of languages. Against this context, the goal of the present section is to provide a thorough examination of both LLMs and MLLMs.
We will discuss the architecture of these models, typically based on the Transformer model (Vaswani et al., [2017](https://arxiv.org/html/2411.11072v1#bib.bib307 "")), as well as other architectures that may have the potential to challenge such supremacy of Transformers. Organized according to the major families of architectures, the deployment of major MLLMs along the last few years are summarized in Figure [2](https://arxiv.org/html/2411.11072v1#S2.F2 "Figure 2 ‣ 2 Taxonomy and Roadmap ‣ Multilingual Large Language Models: A Systematic Survey").

Report issue for preceding element

### 3.1 Dense Transformer

Report issue for preceding element

MLLMs tend typically to adopt the same architecture as monolingual LLMs, even in the era of pre-trained language models (Bendale et al., [2024](https://arxiv.org/html/2411.11072v1#bib.bib24 "")).
However, the finer details of the Transformer architecture can vary significantly when building a top performing language model, which inherently affects the performance and stability of pre-training.

Report issue for preceding element

In an initial period, the preferred architecture was usually either the encoder-only model (Devlin et al., [2018](https://arxiv.org/html/2411.11072v1#bib.bib85 ""); Conneau & Lample, [2019b](https://arxiv.org/html/2411.11072v1#bib.bib64 ""); Conneau et al., [2019](https://arxiv.org/html/2411.11072v1#bib.bib66 ""); Sun et al., [2021](https://arxiv.org/html/2411.11072v1#bib.bib286 "")) or the encoder-decoder model (Lewis et al., [2019](https://arxiv.org/html/2411.11072v1#bib.bib159 ""); Raffel et al., [2020b](https://arxiv.org/html/2411.11072v1#bib.bib243 ""); Xue et al., [2020](https://arxiv.org/html/2411.11072v1#bib.bib350 ""); Costa-jussà et al., [2022](https://arxiv.org/html/2411.11072v1#bib.bib71 "")), both of which typically utilize non-causal masked attention to perform denoising tasks.

Report issue for preceding element

Following the subsequent success of GPT models (Brown et al., [2020a](https://arxiv.org/html/2411.11072v1#bib.bib31 ""); Ouyang et al., [2022a](https://arxiv.org/html/2411.11072v1#bib.bib223 "")), the preferred approach shifted to the decoder-only model, which excel in generation tasks.
Useful pre-training of these models involves training with a substantial number of parameters, say over 7 billion, on a massive amount of tokens, over 1 trillion.
This process requires extensive GPU memory and time, which represents a significant cost.
To address these challenges and enhance the performance of pre-trained models, various modifications have been made to the vanilla Transformers, often related to the self-attention mechanism, layer normalization, activation functions and position embeddings.

Report issue for preceding element

LLaMA (Touvron et al., [2023b](https://arxiv.org/html/2411.11072v1#bib.bib301 "")) is one of the first open foundation models that paved the way for the success of open source MLLMs.
Despite using the vanilla Transformer architecture, LLaMA introduces significant modifications.
It adopts pre-normalization like GPT-3 (Brown et al., [2020a](https://arxiv.org/html/2411.11072v1#bib.bib31 "")), and uses RMSNorm (Zhang & Sennrich, [2019](https://arxiv.org/html/2411.11072v1#bib.bib372 "")) instead of the traditional layer normalization, which eliminates the shift operation of layer normalization and improves FLOPs.
Additionally, LLaMA chooses SwiGLU, following PaLM (Chowdhery et al., [2022](https://arxiv.org/html/2411.11072v1#bib.bib59 "")), to enhance performance, and Rotary Position Embedding (RoPE) (Su et al., [2024](https://arxiv.org/html/2411.11072v1#bib.bib283 "")), following GPTNeo (Black et al., [2021](https://arxiv.org/html/2411.11072v1#bib.bib27 "")), instead of standard absolute position embeddings to support long-context extension.
LLaMA also removes the linear bias of the feed-forward networks and self-attention mechanism. This design approach has been widely adopted by successors such as Yi (Young et al., [2024](https://arxiv.org/html/2411.11072v1#bib.bib364 "")), Deepseek-LLM (Bi et al., [2024](https://arxiv.org/html/2411.11072v1#bib.bib26 "")), InternLM (Team, [2023](https://arxiv.org/html/2411.11072v1#bib.bib294 "")).

Report issue for preceding element

Other MLLMs employ different architectures.
For example, Qwen1.0 (Bai et al., [2023b](https://arxiv.org/html/2411.11072v1#bib.bib18 "")) retains the bias in self-attention, and Gemma uses GeGLU (Team et al., [2024](https://arxiv.org/html/2411.11072v1#bib.bib293 "")) instead of SwiGLU.
Falcon (Almazrouei et al., [2023](https://arxiv.org/html/2411.11072v1#bib.bib12 "")) and BaiChuan-13B (Yang et al., [2023b](https://arxiv.org/html/2411.11072v1#bib.bib354 "")) uses ALiBi (Press et al., [2021](https://arxiv.org/html/2411.11072v1#bib.bib236 "")) instead of RoPE for position embeddings.
To decrease memory usage during inference, Grouped Query Attention (GQA) (Ainslie et al., [2023](https://arxiv.org/html/2411.11072v1#bib.bib8 "")) has been implemented in many LLMs, including LLaMA-2 (Touvron et al., [2023d](https://arxiv.org/html/2411.11072v1#bib.bib303 "")), Yi (Young et al., [2024](https://arxiv.org/html/2411.11072v1#bib.bib364 "")), DeepSeek-LLM (Bi et al., [2024](https://arxiv.org/html/2411.11072v1#bib.bib26 "")), InternLM 2 (Cai et al., [2024](https://arxiv.org/html/2411.11072v1#bib.bib35 "")), and OpenELM (Mehta et al., [2024](https://arxiv.org/html/2411.11072v1#bib.bib198 "")). Compared to Multi-Head Self-Attention (MHA), GQA groups multiple queries and uses a single key and value head, reducing memory usage.

Report issue for preceding element

MLLMs like BLOOM (Le Scao et al., [2023](https://arxiv.org/html/2411.11072v1#bib.bib153 "")) and PolyLM (Wei et al., [2023](https://arxiv.org/html/2411.11072v1#bib.bib325 "")) use the GeLU activation function and vanilla layer normalization, as well as ALiBi instead of RoPE for position embeddings.
These architectural differences are not specific to language, but rather general improvements.
BLOOM also expanded the vocabulary size to 250K to reduce the risk of under-segmenting for multilingual purposes, whereas other monolingual LLMs from the same period used much smaller vocabulary sizes, typically around 32K.
Another MLLM FuxiTranyu (Sun et al., [2024](https://arxiv.org/html/2411.11072v1#bib.bib285 "")) makes a balance between performance and training efficiency, using GeLU activation function and RMSNorm.
Similar to BLOOM, FuxiTranyu expands the vocabulary size to 250K to fit the multilingual corpora.

Report issue for preceding element

Researchers have also proposed new alternatives to MHA or GQA.
For instance, the Mistral-7B model (Jiang et al., [2023](https://arxiv.org/html/2411.11072v1#bib.bib127 "")) adopts Sliding Window Attention (SWA), and DeepSeek-V2 (DeepSeek-AI et al., [2024a](https://arxiv.org/html/2411.11072v1#bib.bib80 "")) proposes Multi-Head Latent Attention (MLA). These variants aim to reduce the KV cache during inference.

Report issue for preceding element

### 3.2 MoE Transformer

Report issue for preceding element

The Mixture of Experts (MoE) architecture is an effective approach for scaling model parameters while keeping the FLOPs similar to their dense counterparts.
Research on MoE models has shown promising results across multiple tasks (Shazeer et al., [2017](https://arxiv.org/html/2411.11072v1#bib.bib263 "")).

Report issue for preceding element

OpenMoE (Xue et al., [2024](https://arxiv.org/html/2411.11072v1#bib.bib349 "")) is one of the first attempts to build an open-sourced LLM adopting an MoE approach, with parameters ranging from 650M to 34B, pre-trained on 1T tokens.
Unlike Switch Transformer or GShard (Fedus et al., [2022](https://arxiv.org/html/2411.11072v1#bib.bib92 ""); Lepikhin et al., [2020](https://arxiv.org/html/2411.11072v1#bib.bib156 "")), which replace the Feed-Forward Network (FFN) module with MoE, OpenMoE interleaves the MoE module with the FFN module.
Mixtral-8x7B (Jiang et al., [2024](https://arxiv.org/html/2411.11072v1#bib.bib128 "")), in turn, is an outstanding LLM that pushes forward the experimentation with MoE.
It adopts an architecture similar to the dense Mistral-7B model, replacing the FFN module with the MoE module.
Mixtral-8x7B contains 8 experts per layer and uses a top-2 routing mechanism to select experts for each token. Xai’s Grok-1 model222https://x.ai/blog/grok follows this setup, scaling the parameters to 314B.

Report issue for preceding element

DeepSeek MoE (Dai et al., [2024](https://arxiv.org/html/2411.11072v1#bib.bib77 "")) employs a similar architecture but with a fine-grained expert design.
The original N𝑁Nitalic\_N experts are segmented into m⁢N𝑚𝑁mNitalic\_m italic\_N experts and correspondingly routed to m⁢K𝑚𝐾mKitalic\_m italic\_K experts instead of K𝐾Kitalic\_K experts to achieve a more flexible combination of activated experts.
Additionally, it leaves Kssubscript𝐾𝑠K\_{s}italic\_K start\_POSTSUBSCRIPT italic\_s end\_POSTSUBSCRIPT experts as shared experts, leading to a final number of routed experts of m⁢K−Ks𝑚𝐾subscript𝐾𝑠mK-K\_{s}italic\_m italic\_K - italic\_K start\_POSTSUBSCRIPT italic\_s end\_POSTSUBSCRIPT while m⁢K𝑚𝐾mKitalic\_m italic\_K experts are activated. Using this MoE architecture, performance similar to their dense counterparts is achieved, with the same total number of parameters.
The Qwen1.5-MoE series (Team, [2024a](https://arxiv.org/html/2411.11072v1#bib.bib295 "")) follows DeepSeek MoE’s successful approach, using 4 shared experts and 4 of 60 activated experts.
DBRX (Team, [2024b](https://arxiv.org/html/2411.11072v1#bib.bib296 "")), in turn, uses a similar idea to build a fine-grained MoE architecture with 16 experts, activating 4 of them.
These fine-grained MoE shows promising results compared to Mixtral-8x7B and Grok-1. However, they do not use shared experts.

Report issue for preceding element

In summary, the MoE approach provides an effective way to scale the parameters of MLLMs, and fine-grained expert design leads to surprisingly good performance compared to dense counterparts.
In the context of multilingual models, the main issue with model architecture is often its limited capabilities.
It remains an open question to be examined whether a fine-grained MoE architecture would significantly boost the performance of MLLMs.

### 3.3 Competitors of Transformer

Report issue for preceding element

Despite the supremacy of the Transformer architecture for MLLMs, it has a significant drawback: its time complexity scales quadratically with the sequence length.
Competitors to the transformer often propose architectures with linear time complexity.

Report issue for preceding element

RWKV (Peng et al., [2023](https://arxiv.org/html/2411.11072v1#bib.bib229 "")) is a variant of the Recurrent Neural Networks (RNN) architecture that stacks residual blocks with time-mixing and channel-mixing modules.
RWKV has scaled to 7 billion parameters and matches Transformer performance on multiple benchmarks.
Mamba (Gu & Dao, [2023](https://arxiv.org/html/2411.11072v1#bib.bib108 "")) follows previous state-space models like S4 and H3 (Gu et al., [2022](https://arxiv.org/html/2411.11072v1#bib.bib109 ""); Fu et al., [2023](https://arxiv.org/html/2411.11072v1#bib.bib97 "")), adopting the state-space architecture while scaling parameters to 1.3 billion.
It has shown promising results on multiple validation sets using perplexity as the metric, although whether it can scale much larger remains unknown.

Report issue for preceding element

Jamba (Lieber et al., [2024](https://arxiv.org/html/2411.11072v1#bib.bib179 "")) can be seen as a successful fusion of Mamba and Transformers, stacking Mamba layers, Mamba with MoE layers, and Transformer layers together.
Jamba inherits the high-quality output of transformers and the high throughput of Mamba, demonstrating remarkable performance on several benchmarks compared to LLaMA-2 70B and Mixtral 8x7B, with a total of 52 billion parameters and 12 billion activated parameters.

## 4 Multilingual Corpora

Report issue for preceding element

Training MLLMs typically involves three major stages: pre-training, supervised fine-tuning (SFT), and reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF).
Pre-training requires vast amounts of unlabeled, raw text, while SFT and RLHF occur during the alignment phase.
The GPT-3 (Brown et al., [2020b](https://arxiv.org/html/2411.11072v1#bib.bib32 "")), based on the transformer architecture, demonstrates strong contextual learning abilities with pre-training using only large amounts of unlabeled data. However, it still shows significant gaps in areas such as value alignment.
The powerful capabilities of ChatGPT arise from quality data used in supervised fine-tuning and intense RLHF (Ouyang et al., [2022b](https://arxiv.org/html/2411.11072v1#bib.bib224 "")).
Subsequently, skillful chat models such as the Qwen-Chat series (Bai et al., [2023a](https://arxiv.org/html/2411.11072v1#bib.bib17 "")), LLaMA-Chat series (Touvron et al., [2023a](https://arxiv.org/html/2411.11072v1#bib.bib300 "")), and Baichuan 2-Chat series (Yang et al., [2023a](https://arxiv.org/html/2411.11072v1#bib.bib353 "")) have emerged, all having undergone both SFT and RLHF.
Consequently, gathering, preparing, curating and handling data deserves and has gained substantial research, as witnessed by the expanding ELRA Language Resources Association’s LREC conferences,333https://www.elra.info/elra-events/lrec/ among others.

Report issue for preceding element

In this section, we will introduce the pre-training and alignment data for MLLMs separately.
For the alignment phase, we will discuss SFT data and RLHF data in detail.

Report issue for preceding element

### 4.1 Multilingual Pre-training Datasets

Report issue for preceding element

Pre-training is the most time-consuming and resource-intensive stage during a typical MLLMs training.
Compared to alignment data, the amount of pre-training data tends to be much larger. Qwen (Bai et al., [2023a](https://arxiv.org/html/2411.11072v1#bib.bib17 "")) has undergone pre-training on 2 to 3 trillion tokens, Baichuan 2 (Yang et al., [2023a](https://arxiv.org/html/2411.11072v1#bib.bib353 "")) on 2.6 trillion tokens, and the LLaMA 3444 [https://ai.meta.com/blog/meta-llama-3](https://ai.meta.com/blog/meta-llama-3 "") model on 15 trillion tokens.
To ensure that the model can learn and generalize across input data during the pre-training stage, the pre-training data encompasses a wide range of fields and sources, and data filtering methods should be employed to ensure its quality.
For MLLMs, a rich collection of multilingual data enables the model to learn connections between languages, and generalize across them, thereby enhancing its multilingual capabilities.

Report issue for preceding element

#### 4.1.1 Multilingual Data from the Web

Report issue for preceding element

Taking into account the sources of data, typically the data can be roughly divided into web crawl, book, code, academic paper, news, and others.

Report issue for preceding element

Considering the distribution of data domains, they can be divided into general and domain-specific data.

Report issue for preceding element

Report issue for preceding element

The most well-known source of pre-training data for MLLMs is CommonCrawl999https://commoncrawl.org, a large-scale collection of web dumps.
It crawls billions of web pages every month and releases a snapshot, now containing snapshots from 2008 to the present, and it is continuously being updated.
CommonCrawl contains web data in multiple languages but includes a lot of pornographic, violent, and misaligned information that needs to be filtered before use.

Report issue for preceding element

Nowadays, many web-based corpora are cleaned and obtained from CommonCrawl.
CC100 (Conneau et al., [2020a](https://arxiv.org/html/2411.11072v1#bib.bib67 "")), mC4 (Xue et al., [2021](https://arxiv.org/html/2411.11072v1#bib.bib351 "")), FineWeb101010https://huggingface.co/spaces/HuggingFaceFW/blogpost-fineweb-v1, RedPajama v2 (Computer, [2023](https://arxiv.org/html/2411.11072v1#bib.bib62 "")), RedPajama (part) (Computer, [2023](https://arxiv.org/html/2411.11072v1#bib.bib62 "")), and SlimPajama (Shen et al., [2023](https://arxiv.org/html/2411.11072v1#bib.bib268 "")) are extracted and filtered from CommonCrawl.
They contain multiple languages and represent the largest data volumes.

Report issue for preceding element

CC100(Conneau et al., [2020a](https://arxiv.org/html/2411.11072v1#bib.bib67 "")) is a dataset gathered from the web with over 100 languages, generated from 12 snapshots of CommonCrawl from the year 2018.
Only one snapshot was used for English, while the other languages were extracted using all 12 snapshots.
This dataset was processed using CCNET (Wenzek et al., [2020](https://arxiv.org/html/2411.11072v1#bib.bib327 "")), an open-source CommonCrawl processing pipeline.
The CCNET processing pipeline includes language identification, deduplication, and filtering based on language model perplexity.

Report issue for preceding element

mC4(Xue et al., [2021](https://arxiv.org/html/2411.11072v1#bib.bib351 "")) is the multilingual version of the C4 dataset, which is primarily aimed at English while mC4 covers 108 languages.
It is extracted and deduplicated from CommonCrawl, followed by filtering based on various rules, including line length etc.

Report issue for preceding element

RedPajama(Computer, [2023](https://arxiv.org/html/2411.11072v1#bib.bib62 "")) was initiated to reproduce the training data for LLama. Most of its data comes from CommonCrawl and C4, with a small portion from code, books, papers, and wikipedias.

Report issue for preceding element

RedPajama v2(Computer, [2023](https://arxiv.org/html/2411.11072v1#bib.bib62 "")) is a large-scale dataset processed using the CCNET pipeline on CommonCrawl, containing data in 5 languages.

Report issue for preceding element

SlimPajama(Shen et al., [2023](https://arxiv.org/html/2411.11072v1#bib.bib268 "")) is a high-quality dataset derived from RedPajama after extensive filtering and deduplication.

Report issue for preceding element

FineWeb is primarily English with a small amount of multilingual data.
It has undergone more meticulous cleaning, including common URL-based filtering and custom filters for removing list-like documents, documents with repeated lines, and documents with potentially incorrect line formats.
After thorough processing, FineWeb’s data quality surpasses other high-quality datasets such as SlimPajama and C4.

Report issue for preceding element

Zyda(Tokpanov et al., [2024](https://arxiv.org/html/2411.11072v1#bib.bib299 "")) dataset, encompassing 1.3 trillion tokens, is a high-quality pre-training dataset created by integrating multiple premium datasets such as RefinedWeb, SlimPajama, C4, and arXiv.
This integration process involved meticulous de-duplication and filtering at a fine-grained level, both within individual datasets and across different datasets.

### 4.2 Multilingual Alignment Datasets

Report issue for preceding element

In this section, we introduce the datasets for so-called alignment.
Alignment is an important research topic as pre-training enables models to acquire knowledge, while alignment allows models to follow instructions and align to human preferences and ethics.
The alignment process for MLLMs is usually divided into two stages: Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) and Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF).

Report issue for preceding element

#### 4.2.1 Datasets for Supervised Fine-Tuning

Report issue for preceding element

SFT involves inputting diverse instructions and producing the respective outputs that align with human preferences.

Report issue for preceding element

Two data-related factors influence the effectiveness of instruction fine-tuning.
First, data quality: high-quality data is more effective than larger quantities of data (Touvron et al., [2023d](https://arxiv.org/html/2411.11072v1#bib.bib303 "")).
Second, the diversity of instructions: a richer variety of instruction types tend to better help the alignment of the models.

Report issue for preceding element

The development of SFT datasets can be categorized into LLM-generated and human-annotated data.
According to LLaMA 2 (Touvron et al., [2023d](https://arxiv.org/html/2411.11072v1#bib.bib303 "")), synthesized SFT data is competitive with human-annotated SFT data. Consequently, a significant portion of SFT data is actually derived from model-assisted generation or entirely model-generated.
This approach allows for the reallocation of substantial human annotation costs to other alignment data, such as RLHF.

Report issue for preceding element

We classify the data into three categories based on the method of synthesis: AI-Generated, Manually-Created, and mixed, and provide an overview of the SFT datasets.

Report issue for preceding element

AI-generated data is produced by MLLMs like GPT-4202020https://openai.com/index/gpt-4/ or others, sometimes using seed instructions or prompts provided by humans. Manually-created data is constructed entirely by humans. Mixed datasets include portions that are manually-created, AI-generated, and data obtained by applying instruction templates to traditional NLP datasets. ## 5 Pre-training

Report issue for preceding element

Thanks to the results obtained by the open-source community, the techniques underlying the pre-training of MLLMs have become increasingly more transparent.
The primary techniques in the pre-training phase of MLLMs revolve around the collection and pre-processing of multilingual data, which takes a dominant role.
Pre-training objectives and strategies are also crucial to their eventual performance.

Report issue for preceding element

### 5.1 Data Curation

Report issue for preceding element

Research has demonstrated that a high-quality, de-duplicated pre-training dataset is essential for the enhanced performance of pre-trained LLMs (Young et al., [2024](https://arxiv.org/html/2411.11072v1#bib.bib364 ""); Lee et al., [2022](https://arxiv.org/html/2411.11072v1#bib.bib155 "")).
Given that a substantial portion of pre-training data is sourced from the web, ensuring the quality and safety of this data is crucial.
The process of developing such dataset for a well-performing LLM can be organized into five parts: language identification, quality filtering, safety filtering, deduplication, and up-sampling of certain domains.

Report issue for preceding element

Language identification is crucial for subsequent filtering methods since heuristic rule filters are typically based on the statistical information of the dataset, which can vary significantly across different languages.

Report issue for preceding element

For quality filtering, combining filters based on heuristic rules with machine learned filters improves data quality as they permit to take into consideration both syntactic and semantic aspects (Young et al., [2024](https://arxiv.org/html/2411.11072v1#bib.bib364 ""); Bi et al., [2024](https://arxiv.org/html/2411.11072v1#bib.bib26 ""); Cai et al., [2024](https://arxiv.org/html/2411.11072v1#bib.bib35 "")).

Report issue for preceding element

Heuristic rule filters often involve filtering documents based on pre-defined block lists, such as URLs, and the statistical information of documents, including character/token/digit/symbol ratios and the frequency of repeated words/n-grams/paragraphs (Young et al., [2024](https://arxiv.org/html/2411.11072v1#bib.bib364 ""); Cai et al., [2024](https://arxiv.org/html/2411.11072v1#bib.bib35 ""); Mehta et al., [2024](https://arxiv.org/html/2411.11072v1#bib.bib198 "")).
These rules are usually designed based on observations of the data. For instance, BLOOM (Le Scao et al., [2023](https://arxiv.org/html/2411.11072v1#bib.bib153 "")) defines a series of indicators to filter out low-quality data for each language, with indicators selected by fluent speakers of each language.

Report issue for preceding element

Learned filters typically involve task-specific trained models.
Examples include using KenLM252525https://github.com/kpu/kenlm to measure document perplexity or trained quality models to score data quality.
For instance, Cai et al. ( [2024](https://arxiv.org/html/2411.11072v1#bib.bib35 "")) organize human annotators to label document quality and fine-tune BERT models to serve as filters.
LLaMA 3 (AI@Meta, [2024](https://arxiv.org/html/2411.11072v1#bib.bib7 "")) finds that using LLaMA 2 to identify high-quality data yield excellent results, and leverages it to generate high-quality text data.

Report issue for preceding element

To enhance the safety of pre-training data, documents containing unsafe content must be filtered out.
Like quality filters, safety filters are composed of manually designed heuristic rules and machine learned filters, targeting, for instance, personally identifiable information (PII), toxicity or unwanted words or domains (Young et al., [2024](https://arxiv.org/html/2411.11072v1#bib.bib364 ""); Cai et al., [2024](https://arxiv.org/html/2411.11072v1#bib.bib35 ""); Bai et al., [2023b](https://arxiv.org/html/2411.11072v1#bib.bib18 ""); Touvron et al., [2023d](https://arxiv.org/html/2411.11072v1#bib.bib303 ""); Team et al., [2024](https://arxiv.org/html/2411.11072v1#bib.bib293 "")).
As another example, (DeepSeek-AI et al., [2024b](https://arxiv.org/html/2411.11072v1#bib.bib81 "")) removes also contentious content from the pre-training corpus to mitigate cultural bias in the data.

Report issue for preceding element

Turning to text deduplication, it significantly impacts LLM performance.
Current deduplication methods include exact-match deduplication and fuzzy-match deduplication, using algorithms like MinHash and LSH (Young et al., [2024](https://arxiv.org/html/2411.11072v1#bib.bib364 ""); Bi et al., [2024](https://arxiv.org/html/2411.11072v1#bib.bib26 ""); Bai et al., [2023b](https://arxiv.org/html/2411.11072v1#bib.bib18 ""); Team, [2023](https://arxiv.org/html/2411.11072v1#bib.bib294 ""); AI@Meta, [2024](https://arxiv.org/html/2411.11072v1#bib.bib7 "")).
Effective deduplication ensures that redundant data does not skew the training process.

Report issue for preceding element

Some dataset were also subject to up-sampling methods for specific domains or data sources to enhance their diversity (Bi et al., [2024](https://arxiv.org/html/2411.11072v1#bib.bib26 ""); Bai et al., [2023b](https://arxiv.org/html/2411.11072v1#bib.bib18 ""); Touvron et al., [2023d](https://arxiv.org/html/2411.11072v1#bib.bib303 "")).
This approach ensures that the pre-training dataset represents a broad range of linguistic and contextual variations.

Most popular MLLMs have increasingly adopted the decoder-only architecture and causal mask attention mechanism.
This focus has led to a corresponding focus in terms of pre-training objectives, moving from masked language modeling to next token prediction.
Under this pre-training objective, MLLMs are trained autoregressively to predict the next token given the current tokens, which can be formulated as:

Besides the next token prediction objectives, masked language modeling tasks can also be used to train LLMs.
UL2 (Tay et al., [2022](https://arxiv.org/html/2411.11072v1#bib.bib292 "")) proposes using a combination of denoising objectives for pre-training.
It includes R-Denoiser, S-Denoiser, and X-Denoiser. R-Denoiser is the standard span corruption introduced in T5 (Raffel et al., [2020b](https://arxiv.org/html/2411.11072v1#bib.bib243 "")), typically masking 15% of the input tokens in spans of 2-5 tokens.
S-Denoiser is akin to prefix language modeling, partitioning the input sequence into two sub-sequences corresponding to source and target.
X-Denoiser is similar to R-Denoiser but with longer spans and a higher corruption rate.

By incorporating these denoisers, UL2 pre-training objectives can be applied to any model architecture.
It has been successfully applied to PaLM-2, showing promising results.
OpenMoE (Xue et al., [2024](https://arxiv.org/html/2411.11072v1#bib.bib349 "")) also experimented with UL2 as the pre-training objective but found that the model’s improvement slowed beyond the early training stage.

### 5.3 Pre-training Strategies

Report issue for preceding element

To fully utilize computing resources during the pre-training stage, packing (Raffel et al., [2020b](https://arxiv.org/html/2411.11072v1#bib.bib243 "")) is used instead of padding, as padding introduces meaningless computation.
Packing involves collecting different sequences into a single document and then truncating it into multiple smaller segments of a predefined sequence length.
However, this method disregards sentence semantics, potentially truncating sentences in the middle or concatenating multiple irrelevant sequences into a single segment.

Report issue for preceding element

Going beyond a single pre-training stage, many MLLMs incorporate a multi-stage pre-training strategy aimed at extending the context length (Cai et al., [2024](https://arxiv.org/html/2411.11072v1#bib.bib35 ""); DeepSeek-AI et al., [2024a](https://arxiv.org/html/2411.11072v1#bib.bib80 "")).
The quadratic complexity of self-attention computation related to context length results in a significant increase in both computation and memory costs.
And implementing a multi-stage pre-training with an expanded long context window has proven to be an effective solution, as this stage requires fewer tokens than the initial stage.

Report issue for preceding element

For example, InternLM 2 (Cai et al., [2024](https://arxiv.org/html/2411.11072v1#bib.bib35 "")) dedicates 90% of total training steps to a 4096 context length, while the remaining 9% of training steps use a 32K context length.

Report issue for preceding element

In addition to the stage that extends context length, MiniCPM (Hu et al., [2024](https://arxiv.org/html/2411.11072v1#bib.bib116 "")) proposes another pre-training strategy to enhance MLLM performance on downstream tasks, called the warmup-stable-decay learning rate scheduler (WSD LRS).
The warmup and stable stages are the same as in conventional pre-training.
In the decay stage, the learning rate rapidly decreases from the maximum to the minimum. The loss curve demonstrates that this strategy achieves significantly better performance compared to the original pre-training strategy.
MiniCPM suggests that 10% of training steps dedicated to the decay stage is sufficient.

## 6 Multilingual Tuning

Report issue for preceding element

There are over 7,000 languages spoken on the planet, yet most existing LLMs are primarily English-based or have limited multilingual capabilities.
This hampers access to cutting-edge Artificial Intelligence for non-English speakers and poses the risk of cultural uniformisation and the loss of linguistic diversity.
To democratize LLMs across languages, a number of efforts have sought to extend tuning of MLLMs to multilingual scenarios.

Report issue for preceding element

As summarized in Figure [3](https://arxiv.org/html/2411.11072v1#S5.F3 "Figure 3 ‣ 5.3 Pre-training Strategies ‣ 5 Pre-training ‣ Multilingual Large Language Models: A Systematic Survey"), in this section, we start by introducing common tuning strategies to adapt the general capabilities of LLMs to specific objectives.
Then, we present two common multilingual tuning strategies.
The first is direct multilingual tuning, which simply expands tuning data to multiple languages; the second focuses on cross-lingual alignment during multilingual tuning, transferring capabilities from the pivot language (primarily English) to other languages.
We will also discuss specific tuning methods used to enhance particular multilingual capabilities.

Report issue for preceding element

### 6.1 Basic Tuning Strategies

Report issue for preceding element

Here we introduce foundational tuning techniques for adapting the general capabilities of MLLMs to specific objectives.
These techniques also serve as the basis for multilingual tuning.
They are: instruction tuning, preference tuning, and continual pre-training.

Report issue for preceding element

#### 6.1.1 Instruction Tuning

Report issue for preceding element

In general, MLLMs are trained using a self-supervised learning objective, which involves predicting a token on the basis of the preceding or surrounding tokens (Brown et al., [2020b](https://arxiv.org/html/2411.11072v1#bib.bib32 ""); Chowdhery et al., [2023](https://arxiv.org/html/2411.11072v1#bib.bib60 ""); Zeng et al., [2021](https://arxiv.org/html/2411.11072v1#bib.bib371 ""); Zhang et al., [2022](https://arxiv.org/html/2411.11072v1#bib.bib379 ""); Scao et al., [2022](https://arxiv.org/html/2411.11072v1#bib.bib256 ""); Rae et al., [2021](https://arxiv.org/html/2411.11072v1#bib.bib240 ""); Touvron et al., [2023a](https://arxiv.org/html/2411.11072v1#bib.bib300 ""); Shaham et al., [2024a](https://arxiv.org/html/2411.11072v1#bib.bib260 "")).
When a prompt is entered, the MLLMs generate a completion for that prompt that is contextually appropriate.
However, despite the appropriateness of these completions, they may not always align with human preferences, thereby limiting the practical applications of MLLMs.
To address this issue, instruction tuning has been proposed, which aims to enhance the alignment of generated responses with human preferences and has become the most widely method adopted to fine-tune MLLMs.

Report issue for preceding element

Instruction tuning is a technique designed to bridge the gap between the next-token prediction objective of MLLMs during pre-training and the goal of providing desired responses for humans in practical scenarios.
Unlike the pre-training stage, which typically involves training the LLMs on document corpora, instruction tuning involves training the models with instructional prompts and corresponding completions.

Report issue for preceding element

The pioneering work on instruction tuning involves fine-tuning MLLMs on instructions paraphrased from samples of various NLP tasks, which substantially enhances the performance of MLLMs on unseen tasks (Wei et al., [2022](https://arxiv.org/html/2411.11072v1#bib.bib324 ""); Sanh et al., [2022a](https://arxiv.org/html/2411.11072v1#bib.bib253 "")). However, fine-tuning MLLMs solely on data from NLP tasks can result in models that excel at completing these tasks rather than effectively interacting with humans.

Report issue for preceding element

Notably, Ouyang et al. ( [2022b](https://arxiv.org/html/2411.11072v1#bib.bib224 "")); Bai et al. ( [2022](https://arxiv.org/html/2411.11072v1#bib.bib19 "")); Askell et al. ( [2021](https://arxiv.org/html/2411.11072v1#bib.bib15 "")) fine-tuned MLLMs with instruction data that more closely align with everyday human instructions.
This type of instruction data can be authored by either humans or LLMs themselves (Wang et al., [2023f](https://arxiv.org/html/2411.11072v1#bib.bib318 ""); Xu et al., [2023a](https://arxiv.org/html/2411.11072v1#bib.bib337 ""); Luo et al., [2023b](https://arxiv.org/html/2411.11072v1#bib.bib193 "")). A critical difference between pre-training and instruction tuning is that the latter employs a prompt template that specifies the roles and tasks for MLLMs, which can be populated with samples to conduct the tuning process. Additionally, while pre-training typically computes loss over all tokens in a training sample, instruction tuning can ignore the loss of prompt tokens (Li et al., [2023g](https://arxiv.org/html/2411.11072v1#bib.bib172 "")).
However, recent studies suggest that optimizing the loss over both prompt tokens and response tokens yields superior performance compared to optimizing the loss over response tokens alone (Shi et al., [2024d](https://arxiv.org/html/2411.11072v1#bib.bib272 ""); Huerta-Enochian & Ko, [2024](https://arxiv.org/html/2411.11072v1#bib.bib120 "")).

Report issue for preceding element

#### 6.1.2 Preference Tuning

Report issue for preceding element

In contrast to instruction tuning, which involves training large language models with instructional prompts and their corresponding completions (Zhang et al., [2023d](https://arxiv.org/html/2411.11072v1#bib.bib377 "")), preference tuning typically employs preference data. This data is generated by annotating the more preferred completion between two options (Bai et al., [2022](https://arxiv.org/html/2411.11072v1#bib.bib19 "")) or by ranking completions according to human preference (Ouyang et al., [2022b](https://arxiv.org/html/2411.11072v1#bib.bib224 "")). Currently, two primary techniques are used for preference tuning: Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF) (Ziegler et al., [2019](https://arxiv.org/html/2411.11072v1#bib.bib407 ""); Stiennon et al., [2020](https://arxiv.org/html/2411.11072v1#bib.bib282 ""); Nakano et al., [2021](https://arxiv.org/html/2411.11072v1#bib.bib210 ""); Ouyang et al., [2022b](https://arxiv.org/html/2411.11072v1#bib.bib224 "")) and Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) (Rafailov et al., [2023](https://arxiv.org/html/2411.11072v1#bib.bib241 "")).

Report issue for preceding element

RLHF comprises three essential steps for training LLMs: (1) training LLMs with instruction tuning, also known as supervised fine-tuning; (2) training a reward model using preference data to predict human preferences; and (3) applying reinforcement learning to further train MLLMs from step 1, thereby enhancing the alignment between MLLMs and human preferences.

Report issue for preceding element

In step 2, the trained reward model produces a scalar reward to quantify the degree of human preference for given completions, where a higher reward denotes greater alignment with human preferences. The parameters θ𝜃\\thetaitalic\_θ of the reward model are optimized based on the assumption that the preference data used for training are sampled from a preference function that adheres to the Bradley-Terry model (Bradley & Terry, [1952](https://arxiv.org/html/2411.11072v1#bib.bib30 "")).

#### 6.1.3 Continual Pre-training

Report issue for preceding element

Pre-trained MLLMs can be further adapted to specific objectives through methods such as instruction tuning and preference tuning.
Continual pre-training serves as an intermediary step between the initial pre-training and task-specific fine-tuning, adapting MLLMs’ general knowledge to specific domains or integrating entirely new knowledge (Shi et al., [2024a](https://arxiv.org/html/2411.11072v1#bib.bib269 ""); Mu et al., [2024b](https://arxiv.org/html/2411.11072v1#bib.bib205 ""); Li et al., [2024f](https://arxiv.org/html/2411.11072v1#bib.bib176 "")).
This process enhances the adaptability of MLLMs to specific tasks, thereby improving task performance.

Report issue for preceding element

The training objective during continual pre-training is next-token prediction, similar to that in the pre-training stage.
However, a significant challenge in continual pre-training is catastrophic forgetting (Shi et al., [2024a](https://arxiv.org/html/2411.11072v1#bib.bib269 "")), which occurs when MLLMs are optimized on the target data that are domain-specific or entirely new compared to the pre-training data.
In essence, this phenomenon arises from the distributional differences between the target data and the original pre-training data. Catastrophic forgetting is a critical issue because it not only erases previously acquired knowledge but also hinders effective knowledge transfer.

Report issue for preceding element

To mitigate catastrophic forgetting, common approaches include replay, regularization, and architecture-based methods.
Specifically, replay-based methods involve incorporating samples from the original training data alongside new target data (Shi et al., [2024b](https://arxiv.org/html/2411.11072v1#bib.bib270 ""); Chaudhry et al., [2019](https://arxiv.org/html/2411.11072v1#bib.bib44 ""); Riemer et al., [2019](https://arxiv.org/html/2411.11072v1#bib.bib250 ""); Buzzega et al., [2020](https://arxiv.org/html/2411.11072v1#bib.bib33 ""); Sarfraz et al., [2023](https://arxiv.org/html/2411.11072v1#bib.bib255 ""); Bang et al., [2021](https://arxiv.org/html/2411.11072v1#bib.bib21 "")). Regularization-based methods impose constraints to minimize discrepancies between updated and original model parameters (Zhou & Cao, [2021](https://arxiv.org/html/2411.11072v1#bib.bib396 ""); Aljundi et al., [2018](https://arxiv.org/html/2411.11072v1#bib.bib10 "")), while architecture-based methods primarily focus on parameter-efficient fine-tuning techniques (Dettmers et al., [2023](https://arxiv.org/html/2411.11072v1#bib.bib84 ""); Xu et al., [2023f](https://arxiv.org/html/2411.11072v1#bib.bib348 ""); Lester et al., [2021](https://arxiv.org/html/2411.11072v1#bib.bib157 ""); Li & Liang, [2021](https://arxiv.org/html/2411.11072v1#bib.bib173 ""); Yang et al., [2024b](https://arxiv.org/html/2411.11072v1#bib.bib356 ""); Wu et al., [2024a](https://arxiv.org/html/2411.11072v1#bib.bib328 ""); Wang et al., [2023e](https://arxiv.org/html/2411.11072v1#bib.bib316 "")).

Report issue for preceding element

### 6.2 Direct Multilingual Tuning

Report issue for preceding element

To democratize MLLMs across languages, many studies directly extend the tuning of MLLMs to multilingual contexts.
The majority of these efforts involve direct multilingual instruction tuning, enabling MLLMs to follow instructions in multiple languages (Lai et al., [2023b](https://arxiv.org/html/2411.11072v1#bib.bib151 ""); Li et al., [2023d](https://arxiv.org/html/2411.11072v1#bib.bib167 ""); Muennighoff et al., [2023b](https://arxiv.org/html/2411.11072v1#bib.bib207 ""); Chen et al., [2023f](https://arxiv.org/html/2411.11072v1#bib.bib53 ""); Shaham et al., [2024b](https://arxiv.org/html/2411.11072v1#bib.bib261 ""); Wei et al., [2023](https://arxiv.org/html/2411.11072v1#bib.bib325 ""); Nguyen et al., [2023b](https://arxiv.org/html/2411.11072v1#bib.bib217 ""); Ji & Chen, [2024](https://arxiv.org/html/2411.11072v1#bib.bib125 ""); Kew et al., [2023](https://arxiv.org/html/2411.11072v1#bib.bib137 ""); Chen et al., [2024b](https://arxiv.org/html/2411.11072v1#bib.bib47 ""); Shen et al., [2024b](https://arxiv.org/html/2411.11072v1#bib.bib266 ""); Chirkova & Nikoulina, [2024](https://arxiv.org/html/2411.11072v1#bib.bib55 ""); Üstün et al., [2024](https://arxiv.org/html/2411.11072v1#bib.bib305 ""); Weber et al., [2024](https://arxiv.org/html/2411.11072v1#bib.bib321 "")), while others focus on multilingual preference tuning, aligning MLLMs with human preferences across multiple languages (Lai et al., [2023b](https://arxiv.org/html/2411.11072v1#bib.bib151 ""); Wu et al., [2024d](https://arxiv.org/html/2411.11072v1#bib.bib331 ""); Shen et al., [2024b](https://arxiv.org/html/2411.11072v1#bib.bib266 "")).
These studies adopt significantly different approaches to collecting multilingual tuning data.
Additionally, the research question of how to effectively stimulate cross-lingual transfer during the multilingual tuning process is widely discussed.

Report issue for preceding element

#### 6.2.1 Multilingual Tuning Data Collection

Report issue for preceding element

Expanding the tuning of MLLMs into multilingual scenarios necessitates the collection of multilingual tuning data.
Here, we’ll outline this process separately for multilingual instruction tuning and multilingual preference tuning.

Report issue for preceding element

##### Multilingual Instruction Tuning

Report issue for preceding element

Combining P3 (Sanh et al., [2022b](https://arxiv.org/html/2411.11072v1#bib.bib254 "")) with 30 other multilingual datasets, Muennighoff et al. ( [2023b](https://arxiv.org/html/2411.11072v1#bib.bib207 "")) created the xP3 dataset, which encompasses 46 languages.
They subsequently translated the English prompts in xP3 into non-English languages using the Google Cloud API, resulting in the xP3-mt dataset.

Report issue for preceding element

Additionally, Bactrian-X (Li et al., [2023d](https://arxiv.org/html/2411.11072v1#bib.bib167 "")) collected 67K English instructions from Alpaca (Taori et al., [2023](https://arxiv.org/html/2411.11072v1#bib.bib290 "")) and Dolly (Conover et al., [2023a](https://arxiv.org/html/2411.11072v1#bib.bib69 "")), which were then translated into 51 languages using Google Translate.
They further employed ChatGPT to generate multilingual responses to mitigate issues such as “translationese” and non-native answer styles.

Report issue for preceding element

In addition to the strategy of first translating instructions and then generating language-specific responses, Phoenix (Chen et al., [2023f](https://arxiv.org/html/2411.11072v1#bib.bib53 "")) included additional data by directly translating instructions and responses using GPT-4.
Their multilingual dataset was also derived from English Alpaca and expanded to over 40 languages.

Report issue for preceding element

Similarly, based on Alpaca, Polylm (Wei et al., [2023](https://arxiv.org/html/2411.11072v1#bib.bib325 "")) leveraged 175 English task seeds from it and iteratively collected and filtered samples for 11 languages using a Self-Instruct (Wang et al., [2023f](https://arxiv.org/html/2411.11072v1#bib.bib318 "")) method.

Report issue for preceding element

SeaLLMs (Nguyen et al., [2023b](https://arxiv.org/html/2411.11072v1#bib.bib217 "")), in turn, focused on nine Southeast Asian languages.
To address the scarcity of Southeast Asian data (3.3%) in their instruction dataset, they adopted a hybrid training strategy, merging the instruction data with multilingual pre-training data to achieve more balanced language ratios.

Report issue for preceding element

In contrast, Üstün et al. ( [2024](https://arxiv.org/html/2411.11072v1#bib.bib305 "")) considered a broader range of languages, 101 in total.
Various methods were employed to construct large-scale multilingual datasets, including aggregating and refining multilingual templates, as well as carefully selecting elusive human annotations from fluent speakers of different languages.
Additionally, data augmentation strategies, such as machine translation and generating synthetic data combined with translation, were also utilized.

Report issue for preceding element

##### Multilingual Preference Tuning

Report issue for preceding element

To gather multilingual preference data, Okapi (Lai et al., [2023b](https://arxiv.org/html/2411.11072v1#bib.bib151 "")) employed a series of procedures.
Initially, they expanded the 52K English Alpaca dataset to 158K using Self-Instruct (Wang et al., [2023f](https://arxiv.org/html/2411.11072v1#bib.bib318 "")) techniques.

Report issue for preceding element

Subsequently, ChatGPT was used to translate both instructions and responses into 26 languages.
After translation, the 52K dataset for each language was first used to perform instruction tuning on MLLMs.
Then, 42K instructions were fed into the instruction-tuned model to sample responses. Finally, ChatGPT was employed to translate the obtained responses back into English and rank preferences, resulting in the final preference data.

Report issue for preceding element

It’s worth noting that they conducted this process separately for each language. Afterward, they used the collected preference data to train a reward model for each language, and further trained a preference-tuned model for each language using the remaining 64K instructions per language.

Report issue for preceding element

#### 6.2.2 Cross-Lingual Transfer Elicitation

Report issue for preceding element

In the process of direct multilingual tuning, effectively stimulating cross-lingual transfer under limited resources is an important research question (Xu et al., [2023e](https://arxiv.org/html/2411.11072v1#bib.bib344 "")).
Here, we introduce how this challenge is addressed in terms of multilingual instruction tuning and multilingual preference tuning, respectively.
Overall, these studies indicate that in direct multilingual tuning, cross-lingual transfer is influenced by factors such as the selection of source languages, linguistic relationships, the number of languages involved, and the scale of multilingual instruction data (Razumovskaia et al., [2024](https://arxiv.org/html/2411.11072v1#bib.bib249 ""); Faisal & Anastasopoulos, [2024](https://arxiv.org/html/2411.11072v1#bib.bib91 ""); Kim et al., [2024b](https://arxiv.org/html/2411.11072v1#bib.bib140 "")).

Report issue for preceding element

##### Multilingual Instruction Tuning

Report issue for preceding element

First, several studies suggest that simply performing monolingual instruction tuning on a single language can lead to certain degrees of zero-shot cross-lingual transfer (Muennighoff et al., [2023b](https://arxiv.org/html/2411.11072v1#bib.bib207 ""); Shaham et al., [2024b](https://arxiv.org/html/2411.11072v1#bib.bib261 ""); Chirkova & Nikoulina, [2024](https://arxiv.org/html/2411.11072v1#bib.bib55 "")). Specifically, Shaham et al. ( [2024b](https://arxiv.org/html/2411.11072v1#bib.bib261 "")) found that various source languages yield varying levels of cross-lingual transfer, with English, Italian, and Spanish demonstrating superior results in their experimental settings, while Chirkova & Nikoulina ( [2024](https://arxiv.org/html/2411.11072v1#bib.bib55 "")) noted that adjusting instruction tuning hyperparameters for multilinguality and using sufficient instruction data can improve zero-shot cross-lingual transfer.

Report issue for preceding element

Furthermore, assuming multilingual instruction data is available, several studies explore key factors to promote cross-lingual transfer, such as the number of languages and the volume of instruction data.
Comparing multilingual and monolingual instruction tuning, Shaham et al. ( [2024b](https://arxiv.org/html/2411.11072v1#bib.bib261 "")) found that replacing even a small number of monolingual (English) training samples (as few as 40) with multilingual ones significantly improves performance on these languages.
This finding aligns with other research (Chen et al., [2024b](https://arxiv.org/html/2411.11072v1#bib.bib47 ""); Weber et al., [2024](https://arxiv.org/html/2411.11072v1#bib.bib321 "")), emphasizing the advantages of multilingual instruction tuning over monolingual instruction tuning, especially in resource-constrained settings.
Additionally, considering the amount of multilingual instruction data, Weber et al. ( [2024](https://arxiv.org/html/2411.11072v1#bib.bib321 "")) suggested that sufficient instruction data is essential for achieving better multilingual performance. It is worth noting, however, that this stands in contrast to the Superficial Alignment Hypothesis (Zhou et al., [2023a](https://arxiv.org/html/2411.11072v1#bib.bib395 "")).

Report issue for preceding element

Regarding the number of languages, it is suggested that including just a few languages (e.g., 2-4) can enhance cross-lingual transfer, especially for languages not encountered during pre-training (Shaham et al., [2024b](https://arxiv.org/html/2411.11072v1#bib.bib261 ""); Kew et al., [2023](https://arxiv.org/html/2411.11072v1#bib.bib137 "")).
However, Ji & Chen ( [2024](https://arxiv.org/html/2411.11072v1#bib.bib125 "")) suggested that increasing the number of languages may further enhance multilingual performance.
They also explored other factors such as language similarity and concluded that the optimal number of languages depends on both language similarity and downstream evaluation.

Report issue for preceding element

##### Multilingual Preference Tuning

Report issue for preceding element

While the aforementioned studies explore cross-lingual transfer in direct multilingual instruction tuning, other works address it in multilingual preference tuning (Chai et al., [2024a](https://arxiv.org/html/2411.11072v1#bib.bib39 "")).
Specifically, Wu et al. ( [2024d](https://arxiv.org/html/2411.11072v1#bib.bib331 "")) found that reward models trained on source languages can be effectively utilized for cross-lingual preference tuning in target languages.
They even observed cases where using reward models from source languages outperforms those trained on target languages, possibly due to a regularization effect.
Additionally, high-resource languages (e.g., English) tend to be more effective in inducing cross-lingual preference transfer than low-resource languages (Wu et al., [2024d](https://arxiv.org/html/2411.11072v1#bib.bib331 ""); Shen et al., [2024b](https://arxiv.org/html/2411.11072v1#bib.bib266 "")).

Report issue for preceding element

### 6.3 Multilingual Tuning Augmented by Cross-Lingual Alignment

Report issue for preceding element

While direct multilingual tuning can enhance the multilingual capabilities of MLLMs to some extent, many approaches augment multilingual tuning with cross-lingual alignment to further improve cross-lingual transfer (Li et al., [2024c](https://arxiv.org/html/2411.11072v1#bib.bib163 ""); Peng & Søgaard, [2024](https://arxiv.org/html/2411.11072v1#bib.bib230 "")).
They typically use English, the best resourced language, as the pivot language, aligning the understanding, reasoning, and generation capabilities of MLLMs in non-English languages with those in English.

Report issue for preceding element

Based on how cross-lingual signals are incorporated to achieve alignment, these works can be classified into two categories: Translation-Assisted Tuning and Cross-Lingual Tuning.

Report issue for preceding element

Specifically, Translation-Assisted Tuning defines auxiliary translation-related tasks and combines it with original multilingual tuning, while Cross-Lingual Tuning transforms multilingual tuning tasks into cross-lingual forms without explicitly relying on translation task.

Report issue for preceding element

It’s worth noting that multilingual tuning here generally refers to multilingual instruction tuning, as most approaches perform cross-lingual alignment at this stage. The only exception is the work done by She et al. ( [2024](https://arxiv.org/html/2411.11072v1#bib.bib264 "")), which models cross-lingual alignment as a preference optimization problem.

Report issue for preceding element

#### 6.3.1 Translation-Assisted Tuning

Report issue for preceding element

Assuming the internal translation capability of MLLMs can facilitate cross-lingual alignment, Translation-Assisted Tuning methods define auxiliary translation-related tasks and combine them with original multilingual tuning.
Such tasks involve machine translation (Ranaldi et al., [2023](https://arxiv.org/html/2411.11072v1#bib.bib246 ""); Zhu et al., [2023b](https://arxiv.org/html/2411.11072v1#bib.bib404 ""); [2024e](https://arxiv.org/html/2411.11072v1#bib.bib405 ""); [2024f](https://arxiv.org/html/2411.11072v1#bib.bib406 "")) or other variations (Zhang et al., [2023c](https://arxiv.org/html/2411.11072v1#bib.bib376 ""); Cahyawijaya et al., [2023](https://arxiv.org/html/2411.11072v1#bib.bib34 "")).

Report issue for preceding element

The most straightforward approach is to convert parallel data into translation instruction format and incorporate them to the original multilingual instruction data. While Ranaldi et al. ( [2023](https://arxiv.org/html/2411.11072v1#bib.bib246 "")) focused on bilingual scenarios, Zhu et al. ( [2023b](https://arxiv.org/html/2411.11072v1#bib.bib404 "")) initially explored the correlation between the scale of translation instructions and translation performance through bilingual training, which subsequently served as a reference for determining the allocation of translation instructions in multilingual settings.

Report issue for preceding element

Specifically, for multilingual reasoning tasks, Zhu et al. ( [2024f](https://arxiv.org/html/2411.11072v1#bib.bib406 "")) proposed translation instruction tuning of parallel reasoning questions (Question Alignment) before English instruction tuning for reasoning tasks, thereby facilitating the transfer of English reasoning capabilities of MLLMs to non-English languages.

Report issue for preceding element

Similarly, starting with Question Alignment, Zhu et al. ( [2024e](https://arxiv.org/html/2411.11072v1#bib.bib405 "")) further integrated general multilingual translation instructions (from English to non-English) with English instruction tuning for reasoning tasks, enhancing the ability of MLLMs to generate multilingual reasoning outputs.

Report issue for preceding element

Other studies explore variations of traditional machine translation tasks and transform them into instruction tuning formats.

Report issue for preceding element

Specifically, Zhang et al. ( [2023c](https://arxiv.org/html/2411.11072v1#bib.bib376 "")) extended translation instruction tuning to a multi-turn interactive setting, aiming to simultaneously enhance the cross-lingual alignment and instruction-following capabilities of MLLMs.

Report issue for preceding element

Additionally, Cahyawijaya et al. ( [2023](https://arxiv.org/html/2411.11072v1#bib.bib34 "")) introduced a cross-lingual semantic similarity task, where LLMs are trained to determine the semantic relationship between two parallel sentences. They also introduced a bilingual denoising task, training MLLMs to reconstruct the target side of input parallel sentences that have been noised.

Report issue for preceding element

#### 6.3.2 Cross-Lingual Tuning

Report issue for preceding element

Without relying on auxiliary translation-related tasks, the approaches in Cross-Lingual Tuning reconstruct multilingual instruction tuning into a cross-lingual form, enhancing the cross-lingual alignment of MLLMs during instruction learning in a more integrated manner (Si et al., [2024](https://arxiv.org/html/2411.11072v1#bib.bib274 "")).

Report issue for preceding element

In (Chai et al., [2024b](https://arxiv.org/html/2411.11072v1#bib.bib40 "")), cross-lingual signals are introduced by specifying instructions in non-English languages and responses in English. Certain tokens in the non-English instructions may be replaced with English to construct code-switched instructions.

Report issue for preceding element

In (Zhang et al., [2023f](https://arxiv.org/html/2411.11072v1#bib.bib383 "")) and (Upadhayay & Behzadan, [2023](https://arxiv.org/html/2411.11072v1#bib.bib304 "")), MLLMs were trained to respond to non-English instructions by first thinking in English and then responding in a non-English language. When the input is a non-English instruction, MLLMs are trained to sequentially output the English translation of the instruction, an English response, and finally a non-English response. The Random Online CoT introduced by Chai et al. ( [2024b](https://arxiv.org/html/2411.11072v1#bib.bib40 "")) serves a similar purpose.

Report issue for preceding element

Other works promote cross-lingual alignment by enhancing the cross-lingual consistency of model responses.
When responses are required to be in English, the Cross-lingual Distillation method introduced by Chai et al. ( [2024b](https://arxiv.org/html/2411.11072v1#bib.bib40 "")) minimizes the difference between generated English responses when inputs are in different languages.
For multilingual responses, She et al. ( [2024](https://arxiv.org/html/2411.11072v1#bib.bib264 "")) employed high-performing multilingual translation models (e.g., NLLB-600M-distilled) to compute cross-lingual consistency between non-English and English responses.
They further framed cross-lingual alignment as a preference optimization problem, utilizing the computed cross-lingual consistency as rewards for preference tuning.

Report issue for preceding element

### 6.4 Enhancement of Specific Multilingual Abilities

Report issue for preceding element

The direct multilingual tuning and cross-lingual alignment discussed above serve as foundational strategies for enhancing MLLMs’ capabilities in multilingual instruction following, preference alignment and complex reasoning (Zhao et al., [2024e](https://arxiv.org/html/2411.11072v1#bib.bib390 "")).
Beyond this, there is interest in more multilingual abilities of MLLMs, including diverse capabilities of understanding and generation. Those specific multilingual abilities can be enhanced using particular techniques, which we will address here.

Report issue for preceding element

We will focus on three of such abilities: adaptation to new languages, machine translation and cultural adaptation, as they inherently involve multiple languages or cultures.
Adaptation to new languages primarily involves adapting English-centric MLLMs to other languages; machine translation focuses on translating between different languages; and cultural adaptation addresses the cultural diversity of our society, with language considered one of the proxies of culture.

Report issue for preceding element

#### 6.4.1 Adaptation to New Languages

Report issue for preceding element

Although the techniques employed for adaptation to new languages are general, primarily focusing on vocabulary expansion and continual pre-training, the target languages for adaptation vary across different works (Cui et al., [2023c](https://arxiv.org/html/2411.11072v1#bib.bib76 ""); Kim et al., [2024a](https://arxiv.org/html/2411.11072v1#bib.bib139 ""); Fujii et al., [2024](https://arxiv.org/html/2411.11072v1#bib.bib98 ""); Lin et al., [2024](https://arxiv.org/html/2411.11072v1#bib.bib182 ""); Nguyen et al., [2023a](https://arxiv.org/html/2411.11072v1#bib.bib216 "")).

Report issue for preceding element

For instance, Cui et al. ( [2023c](https://arxiv.org/html/2411.11072v1#bib.bib76 "")) aimed to extend English-based LLMs to Chinese.
To enhance the efficiency of MLLMs in encoding and decoding Chinese text, they trained an additional tokenizer on Chinese corpora before conducting continual pre-training, expanding the original vocabulary of MLLMs.

Report issue for preceding element

Other studies extend the vocabulary and perform continual pre-training on different target languages, such as Korean (Kim et al., [2024a](https://arxiv.org/html/2411.11072v1#bib.bib139 "")), Japanese (Fujii et al., [2024](https://arxiv.org/html/2411.11072v1#bib.bib98 "")), or multiple languages (Lin et al., [2024](https://arxiv.org/html/2411.11072v1#bib.bib182 ""); Nguyen et al., [2023a](https://arxiv.org/html/2411.11072v1#bib.bib216 "")), and so forth.

Report issue for preceding element

Additionally, Kim et al. ( [2024a](https://arxiv.org/html/2411.11072v1#bib.bib139 "")) proposed a seven-stage continuous pre-training strategy to enable LLMs to better learn new token representations.

Report issue for preceding element

Adaptation to new languages presents a significant challenge when data for the target languages are not available.

Report issue for preceding element

In one such case, to enable monolingual instruction-tuned MLLMs to perform multilingual mathematical reasoning tasks, Yoon et al. ( [2024](https://arxiv.org/html/2411.11072v1#bib.bib363 "")) employed an external multilingual encoder and initialized a trainable linear layer as a bridge between the encoder and the MLLMs.
They enhanced them with multilingual understanding capabilities by aligning the representation space of this encoder and the MLLMs.

Report issue for preceding element

In another case, considering the high computational and data resource costs of the strategy of first expanding the vocabulary and then performing continual pre-training, Husain et al. ( [2024](https://arxiv.org/html/2411.11072v1#bib.bib121 "")) advocated for more efficient reuse of the original vocabulary rather than for expanding it.
Given that English-centric vocabularies primarily consist of Roman letters, they proposed romanizing the text of new languages.
Factors considered in this romanization scheme include the similarity between the romanized text and the typical writing style, compatibility with the original LLM tokenizer, and the lossiness of the conversion process.

Report issue for preceding element

Other studies conduct comparative analyses of key techniques for adapting to new languages (Yong et al., [2023b](https://arxiv.org/html/2411.11072v1#bib.bib362 ""); Zhao et al., [2024a](https://arxiv.org/html/2411.11072v1#bib.bib385 ""); Cui & Yao, [2024](https://arxiv.org/html/2411.11072v1#bib.bib75 "")).

Report issue for preceding element

Specifically, Yong et al. ( [2023b](https://arxiv.org/html/2411.11072v1#bib.bib362 "")) compared three languages adaptation strategies, viz. continual pre-training, MAD-X (Pfeiffer et al., [2020](https://arxiv.org/html/2411.11072v1#bib.bib232 "")), and (IA)3superscriptIA3(\\mathrm{IA})^{3}( roman\_IA ) start\_POSTSUPERSCRIPT 3 end\_POSTSUPERSCRIPT(Liu et al., [2022](https://arxiv.org/html/2411.11072v1#bib.bib186 "")), and experimentally found that adapter-based methods are more effective than continual pre-training for MLLMs.

Report issue for preceding element

On the other hand, Zhao et al. ( [2024a](https://arxiv.org/html/2411.11072v1#bib.bib385 "")) investigated the suitability of vocabulary expansion, concluding that such an extension may not be advantageous when the scale of the training dataset is below billions of tokens.

Report issue for preceding element

Similar to (Zhao et al., [2024a](https://arxiv.org/html/2411.11072v1#bib.bib385 "")), Cui & Yao ( [2024](https://arxiv.org/html/2411.11072v1#bib.bib75 "")) suggested that while expanding the vocabulary for new languages may accelerate encoding efficiency, it may not necessarily improve performance.
They also gathered empirical evidence that training from a base model rather than an instruction-tuned model could result in better languages adaptation.

Report issue for preceding element

#### 6.4.2 Machine Translation

Report issue for preceding element

Many works use MLLMs to implements machine translation task (Zhu et al., [2024b](https://arxiv.org/html/2411.11072v1#bib.bib400 ""); [d](https://arxiv.org/html/2411.11072v1#bib.bib402 ""); Cui et al., [2024](https://arxiv.org/html/2411.11072v1#bib.bib74 ""); Zhu et al., [2024c](https://arxiv.org/html/2411.11072v1#bib.bib401 ""); Chen et al., [2024a](https://arxiv.org/html/2411.11072v1#bib.bib45 ""); Zhang et al., [2024a](https://arxiv.org/html/2411.11072v1#bib.bib374 "")).
To adapt MLLMs to machine translation, Yang et al. ( [2023c](https://arxiv.org/html/2411.11072v1#bib.bib357 "")) utilized extensive parallel corpora (exceeding 300M) for fine-tuning.

Report issue for preceding element

However, it has been observed that using excessive parallel data (e.g., 5M or 20M) for translation task training on well pre-trained MLLMs can have adverse effects, potentially due to catastrophic forgetting (Xu et al., [2023b](https://arxiv.org/html/2411.11072v1#bib.bib339 "")).
To address this issue, Xu et al. ( [2023b](https://arxiv.org/html/2411.11072v1#bib.bib339 "")) proposed a two-stage fine-tuning approach. Initially, they conducted continual pre-training on the languages involved in the translation task to enhance MLLMs’ proficiency in those languages.
Then, they performed translation instruction tuning on a small scale (e.g., 58K) but with high-quality parallel data.

Report issue for preceding element

Other studies (Li et al., [2023e](https://arxiv.org/html/2411.11072v1#bib.bib169 ""); Zhu et al., [2024a](https://arxiv.org/html/2411.11072v1#bib.bib399 "")) conducted detailed analyses on multilingual translation instruction tuning, taking into account factors such as language similarity, the volume of pre-training and instruction tuning data, and the translation directions.

Report issue for preceding element

Although commonly used to enhance MLLMs’ translation capabilities, translation instruction tuning is regarded as having certain limitations.
On the one hand, the quality of translation instruction data can restrict the performance of MLLMs (Xu et al., [2024a](https://arxiv.org/html/2411.11072v1#bib.bib340 "")).
On the other hand, MLLMs fine-tuned with translation instructions may overlook specific contextual knowledge, forget instructions, and consequently encounter issues such as hallucinations, over-translation or translation omissions (Wu et al., [2024c](https://arxiv.org/html/2411.11072v1#bib.bib330 ""); Zeng et al., [2024](https://arxiv.org/html/2411.11072v1#bib.bib370 ""); Chen et al., [2023a](https://arxiv.org/html/2411.11072v1#bib.bib48 "")).

Report issue for preceding element

To address these challenges, some efforts have opted for preference tuning to further enhance the translation capabilities of MLLMs.

Report issue for preceding element

To build preference pairs, Xu et al. ( [2024a](https://arxiv.org/html/2411.11072v1#bib.bib340 "")) employed different MLLMs to sample translation results, which were then scored by reference-free evaluation models.

Report issue for preceding element

To efficiently collect high-quality preference data, Xu et al. ( [2024b](https://arxiv.org/html/2411.11072v1#bib.bib342 "")) aligned multilingual versions of books to acquire human translations, forming preference pairs alongside machine-generated translations.

Report issue for preceding element

Additionally, Wu et al. ( [2024c](https://arxiv.org/html/2411.11072v1#bib.bib330 "")) utilized external word aligners to annotate the degree of word alignment for translation candidates, while Zeng et al. ( [2024](https://arxiv.org/html/2411.11072v1#bib.bib370 "")) employed output comparison and preference comparison strategies to construct preference data.

Report issue for preceding element

Instead of performing preference tuning, Chen et al. ( [2023a](https://arxiv.org/html/2411.11072v1#bib.bib48 "")) proposed to strengthen the global representations of instructions, aiming to mitigate MLLMs’ tendency to forget instructions.

Report issue for preceding element

The lack of cross-lingual alignment may also affect machine translation. To enhance cross-lingual alignment, Gao et al. ( [2024](https://arxiv.org/html/2411.11072v1#bib.bib103 "")) introduced XConST, which employs Kullback-Leibler (KL) regularization on semantically equivalent parallel sentences.

Report issue for preceding element

Furthermore, Mao & Yu ( [2024](https://arxiv.org/html/2411.11072v1#bib.bib196 "")) initially utilized external tools to extract statistical word alignment signals and then trained MLLMs to discern these signals.

Report issue for preceding element

Fu et al. ( [2024](https://arxiv.org/html/2411.11072v1#bib.bib96 "")) proposed Relay Decoding, a method aligning two LLMs supporting the source and target languages by training a straightforward mapping layer.

Report issue for preceding element

Additionally, Yang et al. ( [2024a](https://arxiv.org/html/2411.11072v1#bib.bib355 "")) proposed m3P, a multimodal neural machine translation framework to bridge language disparities through universal visual features.

Report issue for preceding element

#### 6.4.3 Cultural Adaptation

Report issue for preceding element

As research continues to advance MLLMs in their capabilities, assessing and enriching their cultural and value diversity becomes increasingly crucial, especially considering their extensive utilization across diverse populations worldwide (Sorensen et al., [2024](https://arxiv.org/html/2411.11072v1#bib.bib278 "")).

Report issue for preceding element

Significant efforts have been dedicated to exploring the multicultural knowledge embedded within LLMs, as well as the extent of their cultural adaptation and alignment (AlKhamissi et al., [2024](https://arxiv.org/html/2411.11072v1#bib.bib11 ""); Naous et al., [2023](https://arxiv.org/html/2411.11072v1#bib.bib211 ""); Liu et al., [2023](https://arxiv.org/html/2411.11072v1#bib.bib184 ""); Arora et al., [2022](https://arxiv.org/html/2411.11072v1#bib.bib13 ""); Report issue for preceding element

However, efforts to fine-tune MLLMs for cultural adaptation are relatively sparse, or limited to English.

Report issue for preceding element

Recently, Li et al. ( [2024a](https://arxiv.org/html/2411.11072v1#bib.bib161 "")) introduced CultureLLM, a methodology aimed at instilling MLLMs with cultural differences.
First, they collected seed data from the World Values Survey (Survey, [2022](https://arxiv.org/html/2411.11072v1#bib.bib287 "")), spanning 9 cultures, and utilized GPT-4 for data augmentation. Subsequently, they fine-tuned LLMs on the augmented data, creating culture-specific models for each culture alongside a unified model.

Report issue for preceding element

Furthermore, Xu et al. ( [2024c](https://arxiv.org/html/2411.11072v1#bib.bib345 "")) proposed CultureSPA, a framework that achieves pluralistic cultural alignment in MLLMs by leveraging their internal cultural knowledge. This framework involves generating diverse questions from seed prompts, yielding both culture-unaware and culture-aware MLLM outputs, collecting culture-related QA pairs and conducting culture-joint and specific SFT. They validated the effectiveness of the method across 18 cultures spanning five continents.

Report issue for preceding element

With a proposed technique for extracting culture-related instruction data from unstructured data, Mukherjee et al. ( [2024](https://arxiv.org/html/2411.11072v1#bib.bib208 "")) performed instruction tuning on this data to enhance the cultural reasoning abilities of MLLMs.

Report issue for preceding element

Despite recognizing that language often acts as a proxy for culture (Hershcovich et al., [2022](https://arxiv.org/html/2411.11072v1#bib.bib114 "")), these works employed English for data collection, leaving exploration in multilingual contexts for future research.

Report issue for preceding element

Other works analyze the relationship between cultural adaptation and multilingual instruction tuning (Choenni et al., [2024](https://arxiv.org/html/2411.11072v1#bib.bib58 ""); Wang et al., [2024a](https://arxiv.org/html/2411.11072v1#bib.bib310 "")).

Report issue for preceding element

Specifically, Choenni et al. ( [2024](https://arxiv.org/html/2411.11072v1#bib.bib58 "")) conducted multilingual instruction tuning using the translated Alpaca dataset, investigating the influence of language-specific instruction tuning and pre-training data on cultural adaptation, as well as the optimal method to elicit cultural knowledge from MLLMs.

Report issue for preceding element

In turn, Wang et al. ( [2024a](https://arxiv.org/html/2411.11072v1#bib.bib310 "")) explored the impact of selected languages and data sources on the shift of cultural values during model fine-tuning.

The evaluation of MLLMs are crucial to have a better understanding towards their performance and capabilities, being also important to assess human-values compliance and to address safety concerns (Zhang et al., [2024d](https://arxiv.org/html/2411.11072v1#bib.bib382 ""); Park et al., [2024](https://arxiv.org/html/2411.11072v1#bib.bib228 ""); Shen et al., [2024a](https://arxiv.org/html/2411.11072v1#bib.bib265 ""); Doddapaneni et al., [2024](https://arxiv.org/html/2411.11072v1#bib.bib88 "")).
In multilingual contexts, the evaluation should be broaden towards diverse languages, where the performance towards each language should be understandable.
In this section, we discuss the multilingual evaluation of MLLMs, focusing on tokenizers, benchmarks and datasets, multilingualism of MLLMs, and MLLMs as multilingual evaluators.
The framework in this section is shown in Figure [4](https://arxiv.org/html/2411.11072v1#S7.F4 "Figure 4 ‣ 7 Multilingual Evaluation ‣ Multilingual Large Language Models: A Systematic Survey").

### 7.1 Multilingual Tokenizer Evaluation

Report issue for preceding element

A tokenizer plays an important role for supporting multilingual processes in LLMs, as tokenizers separate sentences into tokens and map them into numerical ids that are the input for MLLMs.
Tokenizers that supports multilingual tokens are crucial to enhance the performance of MLLMs.

Report issue for preceding element

The fertility of a tokenizer is a metric aimed at assessing its quality, which is defined as the average number of sub-words produced per tokenized word (Rust et al., [2021](https://arxiv.org/html/2411.11072v1#bib.bib252 "")). A lower fertility score indicates a better quality tokenizer.
Fertility is also known as the tokenizer’s compression rate (Xue et al., [2022](https://arxiv.org/html/2411.11072v1#bib.bib352 "")).

Report issue for preceding element

Fertility tests have been conducted to evaluate tokenizers on multilingual sentences across various MLLMs, including BLOOM (Scao et al., [2022](https://arxiv.org/html/2411.11072v1#bib.bib256 "")) and OpenAI models (Ahuja et al., [2023a](https://arxiv.org/html/2411.11072v1#bib.bib5 "")). Based on their findings, the fertility score of OpenAI tokenizers is higher in low-resource languages compared to BLOOM’s tokenizer.

Report issue for preceding element

Another way to evaluate a tokenizer is using parity, which is introduced in (Petrov et al., [2023](https://arxiv.org/html/2411.11072v1#bib.bib231 "")) and it is motivated by the unequal treatment of tokenization across different languages. For instance, a Japanese kanji character can be tokenized into three tokens in GPT-2. To address this issue, the concept of tokenizer parity is introduced to evaluate how fairly tokenizers treat equivalent sentences in different languages.
A tokenizer achieves parity when the ratio of the tokenization results for a sentence in language A compared to a sentence in language B is almost equal to 1.

Report issue for preceding element

A comprehensive evaluation of tokenizers was undertaken by Ali et al. ( [2023](https://arxiv.org/html/2411.11072v1#bib.bib9 "")), dividing the assessment into intrinsic and extrinsic evaluations.

Report issue for preceding element

The intrinsic evaluation focuses solely on metrics like fertility and parity.

Report issue for preceding element

The extrinsic evaluation evaluates the impact of the tokenizer on the performance of LLMs, with respect to downstream tasks performance and computational costs.

Report issue for preceding element

The research found that tokenizers trained with a balanced share across languages achieve better fertility and parity scores. The impact of worst, higher fertility will increase computational costs.

Report issue for preceding element

The evaluation of MLLMs should cover various dimensions, including accuracy, alignment with human values and safety.
In the context of multilingual evaluation, these dimensions should be evaluated for each language, from high-resource to low-resource languages.
In this section, we divide the evaluation benchmarks of MLLMs into a holistic evaluation and a task-specific, alignment and safety evaluation.
We summarize the available datasets in Table [3](https://arxiv.org/html/2411.11072v1#S7.T3 "Table 3 ‣ 7.2 Multilingual Evaluation Benchmarks and Datasets ‣ 7 Multilingual Evaluation ‣ Multilingual Large Language Models: A Systematic Survey").
