##### Languages

Report issue for preceding element

La Leaderboardcontains 22 evaluation datasets in Spanish, including the varieties of Spain, Mexico, Argentina, Chile, and Uruguay. It also gathers datasets in all the official languages of Spain, with 18 datasets in Catalan, 17 in Basque, and 9 in Galician.

Report issue for preceding element

##### Origin

Report issue for preceding element

We aim to evaluate models with high-quality datasets that reflect the cultural and linguistic idiosyncrasies of each language.
For this reason, we only include datasets that have been annotated or revised by at least one native speaker of the language.
We prioritize the inclusion of datasets originally created in the language they evaluate, which constitute 55% of the leaderboard. When this is not possible and translation is required, we prioritize datasets translated by human professionals. Not only does this prevent the loss of linguistic nuances that happens with machine translation Plaza et al. ( [2024](https://arxiv.org/html/2507.00999v1#bib.bib80 "")), but it also allows translators to adapt the text to the target culture Nangia et al. ( [2020](https://arxiv.org/html/2507.00999v1#bib.bib75 "")) and to identify errors in the source datasets and ensure that no extra hints regarding the answer are given in the input prompt Baucells et al. ( [2025](https://arxiv.org/html/2507.00999v1#bib.bib11 "")). In La Leaderboard, 38% of the datasets have been manually translated from an existing English benchmark. We also acknowledge that, given the low-resource nature of some languages we cover, machine translation is more affordable than human translation. However, we only include such datasets if the automatic translation was comprehensively reviewed by a person proficient in the target language. Only 7% of the datasets in La Leaderboardare manual reviews of machine-translated datasets.

Report issue for preceding element

##### Format

Report issue for preceding element

The multiple-choice question-answering (MCQA) format is widely used for automatic evaluations due to its simplicity. Thus, MCQA is the format of 59% of the tasks included in La Leaderboard. We acknowledge that the literature has identified some issues with MCQA tasks, such as models’ sensitivity to answer order Pezeshkpour and Hruschka ( [2024](https://arxiv.org/html/2507.00999v1#bib.bib79 "")); Mina et al. ( [2025](https://arxiv.org/html/2507.00999v1#bib.bib73 "")) or lack of task understanding Khatun and Brown ( [2024](https://arxiv.org/html/2507.00999v1#bib.bib53 "")). Moreover, some suggest that this type of task does not reflect the actual models’ responses and capabilities Li et al. ( [2024](https://arxiv.org/html/2507.00999v1#bib.bib60 "")); Wang et al. ( [2024a](https://arxiv.org/html/2507.00999v1#bib.bib103 "")). To address this issue, we also include text generation tasks, such as summarization, evaluated using NoticIA for Spanish, caBreu for Catalan, and Summarization-GL for Galician. We evaluate long-form question-answering
in Spanish using the AQuAS and RagQuAS datasets. Finally, we assess counter-narrative generation with RefutES in Spanish and CONAN in Basque and Spanish.

Report issue for preceding element

##### Domains

Report issue for preceding element

La Leaderboardincludes well-known generalist datasets aimed at evaluating a model’s capability to understand and complete a task, such as Belebele, WNLI, and XStoryCloze. We also include evaluation datasets focused on truthfulness assessment, such as VeritasQA and the Galician translation of TruthfulQA. There are, in addition, several domains represented in La Leaderboard, such as the medical (e.g., ClinTreatES), legal (e.g., SpaLawEx),
and press (e.g., caBreu, NoticIA). We also include ethics-oriented datasets, evaluating stereotype generation in Spanish and Catalan with CrowsPairs.

Report issue for preceding element

##### Tasks

Report issue for preceding element

The types of tasks chosen for our leaderboard extend those usually included in well-known leaderboards (e.g., reasoning, natural language inference, question answering or summarization) to other task types for which high-quality datasets exist in our target languages
(e.g., counter-narrative generation or linguistic acceptability).
For consistent performance comparisons across languages, we prioritize tasks available in multiple languages.

Report issue for preceding element

#### 3.2.2 Metrics

Report issue for preceding element

The MCQA tasks are evaluated by measuring the logarithmic probabilities (LogProbs) of models’ outputs among a restricted list of options.
For text generation tasks, we compare the expected (gold-standard) and given responses using various metrics depending on the original authors’ implementation, including BLEU (Papineni et al., [2002](https://arxiv.org/html/2507.00999v1#bib.bib78 "")), ROUGE (Lin, [2004](https://arxiv.org/html/2507.00999v1#bib.bib63 "")) and Semantic Answer Similarity (SAS, Risch et al., [2021](https://arxiv.org/html/2507.00999v1#bib.bib86 "")).
Furthermore, following the recent trend of evaluating text generation tasks using LLMs, we are adapting an automated Judge-LLM metric from Zubiaga et al. ( [2024](https://arxiv.org/html/2507.00999v1#bib.bib108 "")).
Since SAS and LLM-based metrics are not currently supported in the evaluation suite we use, the LM Evaluation Harness (Gao et al., [2021](https://arxiv.org/html/2507.00999v1#bib.bib36 "")), we implement them in our open-source fork777 [https://github.com/somosnlp/lm-evaluation-harness](https://github.com/somosnlp/lm-evaluation-harness "").

### 3.4 Efficiency Considerations

Report issue for preceding element

#### 3.4.1 Number of Few-Shot Examples

Report issue for preceding element

Recent literature reveals significant inconsistency in the number of examples (shots) used when evaluating large language models (LLMs). While early research demonstrated notable performance improvements with 3-5 in-context examples Brown et al. ( [2020](https://arxiv.org/html/2507.00999v1#bib.bib16 "")), current evaluation practices vary considerably across different models and benchmarks. For instance, the Open LLM Leaderboard employs 0-5 shots depending on the task, Mistral-7B generally follows this range with an exception of 8 shots for GSM8K Cobbe et al. ( [2021](https://arxiv.org/html/2507.00999v1#bib.bib20 "")), and Llama 3 and OLMo models focus primarily on zero-shot evaluation. In contrast, Gemini models use a broader range of 0-10 shots, including “variable-shot” configurations. This variation extends to language-specific models, with Salamandra101010 [https://hf.co/BSC-LT/salamandra-7b-instruct](https://hf.co/BSC-LT/salamandra-7b-instruct "") and Latxa Etxaniz et al. ( [2024](https://arxiv.org/html/2507.00999v1#bib.bib30 "")) families using different shot configurations in their evaluations, typically ranging from 0 to 5 shots.

Report issue for preceding element

Given this myriad of options, when choosing the number of shots to use in La Leaderboard, we take into consideration the following aspects:

Report issue for preceding element

A. Base vs. instruct models
The number of shots should allow for a fair evaluation of the base models without helping instruct models too much.
Also, the availability of structured datasets in specific evaluation formats—such as MCQA—is very low in mid- and low-resource languages.
This means that models trained on English-heavy corpora are more likely to have encountered these structured formats in English than in other languages, potentially biasing their performance.

Report issue for preceding element

B. Cognitive bias
Models suffer from cognitive bias depending on the order and options presented as few-shots Zhao et al. ( [2021](https://arxiv.org/html/2507.00999v1#bib.bib106 "")); Pezeshkpour and Hruschka ( [2024](https://arxiv.org/html/2507.00999v1#bib.bib79 "")); Mina et al. ( [2025](https://arxiv.org/html/2507.00999v1#bib.bib73 "")). Thus, we ensure that, in MCQA tasks, all possible correct options are included in the in-context learning instances. For example, in an MCQA task with four possible answers, we evaluate on a 4-shot setting, with each shot showing one of the four options as correct, in random order. This is done unless it interferes with item A.

Report issue for preceding element

C. Context windows
The context window limitations of language models vary significantly based on hardware constraints and architectural choices, affecting their ability to process long-form tasks such as summarization and reading comprehension. For example, while the Spanish government’s 40B-parameter ALIA model111111 [https://hf.co/BSC-LT/ALIA-40b](https://hf.co/BSC-LT/ALIA-40b "") operates with a 4,096-token context window, Meta’s Llama 3.2 1B model can handle up to 128K tokens121212 [https://ai.meta.com/blog/llama-3-2-connect-2024-vision-edge-mobile-devices](https://ai.meta.com/blog/llama-3-2-connect-2024-vision-edge-mobile-devices ""). To ensure fair evaluation across models with different context window capacities, few-shot examples are employed with a maximum limit of 2,048 tokens, following the methodology established in previous research on LLM analysis Biderman et al. ( [2023](https://arxiv.org/html/2507.00999v1#bib.bib15 "")).

Report issue for preceding element

D. Prompt format
The evaluation methodology employed task-specific prompts from the LM Evaluation Harness, with new prompts created for previously unimplemented tasks following established formats and validated by dataset authors. The number of few-shots varied based on prompt complexity: convoluted prompts (e.g., paraphrasing with PAWS and reasoning with COPA) used 3 in-context examples to allow models to understand the task while complying with items A and C Brown et al. ( [2020](https://arxiv.org/html/2507.00999v1#bib.bib16 "")); straightforward question-answering tasks employed 2-shot evaluation, while tasks with explicit, naturally structured prompts (like ClinDiagnosES and NoticIA) and those evaluating sentence continuation probability (e.g., XStoryCloze) were conducted using 0-shot evaluation.

Report issue for preceding element

## 4 Evaluation Results and Analysis

Report issue for preceding element

We focus on evaluating models accessible to the broader community. We select 50 open-weights models from various families, primarily ranging from 1B to 9B parameters, while including larger quantized models. We consider multilingual models trained by large technological companies and startups like
Meta-Llama
Grattafiori et al. ( [2024](https://arxiv.org/html/2507.00999v1#bib.bib41 "")) and Mistral Jiang et al. ( [2023](https://arxiv.org/html/2507.00999v1#bib.bib52 ""))
as well as models such as EuroLLM Martins et al. ( [2024](https://arxiv.org/html/2507.00999v1#bib.bib69 "")) and Salamandra151515 [https://hf.co/collections/BSC-LT/salamandra-66fc171485944df79469043a](https://hf.co/collections/BSC-LT/salamandra-66fc171485944df79469043a ""), which
have been designed by European and Spanish research groups specifically to process our target languages more efficiently and capture cultural nuances. We assess both the base and instruction-tuned versions when available (Appendix [C](https://arxiv.org/html/2507.00999v1#A3 "Appendix C Models Evaluated ‣ La Leaderboard: A Large Language Model Leaderboard for Spanish Varieties and Languages of Spain and Latin America")).
Each model-task pair was evaluated once, and the raw, pre-normalization results analyzed in this work are publicly available161616 [https://hf.co/datasets/la-leaderboard/results](https://hf.co/datasets/la-leaderboard/results "").

### 4.1 Model performance

Report issue for preceding element

Table [3](https://arxiv.org/html/2507.00999v1#S3.T3 "Table 3 ‣ 3.4.2 Measuring Model Efficiency ‣ 3.4 Efficiency Considerations ‣ 3 La Leaderboard ‣ La Leaderboard: A Large Language Model Leaderboard for Spanish Varieties and Languages of Spain and Latin America") shows that the models most consistently ranking in the top 10 across languages are Gemma-2-9B base and instructed, Llama-3.1-8B-IT, and the quantized versions of Qwen-2.5-IT 14B and 32B. When prioritizing transparency, EuroLLM-9B stands out, followed by Salamandra-7B. For resource-constrained settings, Salamandra-2B and Qwen-2.5-1.5B offer the best performance.

![Refer to caption](https://arxiv.org/html/2507.00999v1/extracted/6586973/images/barplot_performance_per_task_type.png)Figure 2: Results per type of task type and language.Report issue for preceding element

##### Performance per task

Report issue for preceding element

As illustrated in Figure [2](https://arxiv.org/html/2507.00999v1#S4.F2 "Figure 2 ‣ 4.1 Model performance ‣ 4 Evaluation Results and Analysis ‣ La Leaderboard: A Large Language Model Leaderboard for Spanish Varieties and Languages of Spain and Latin America"), the evaluation results are generally better for NLI tasks, including textual entailment and paraphrasing, and worse for language proficiency tests, with all four languages having similar performance on both tasks. Within the language proficiency tests, which combine reading comprehension, linguistic acceptability, and summarization, results are particularly low for summarization tasks.
In question answering and reasoning tasks, there is a larger inter-language difference, with Galician having significantly lower scores overall, while Basque obtains the best results for reasoning but the second worst for question answering.
While commonsense reasoning results are generally good, math reasoning yields the lowest results, which could be related to a too strict metric (exact match).
Further analysis is needed to understand whether these differences are due to the datasets used or indeed to the models’ performance. The poor results on language proficiency tests also warrant a detailed examination to understand their implications, as they may indicate fundamental limitations in the models’ knowledge across languages.

Report issue for preceding element

##### Performance per language

Report issue for preceding element

Regarding specific models, the same five (Gemma2, Llama3.1, and quantized Qwen2.5) consistently rank among the top ten performers. However, we find that some models stand out for specific language-task pairs.
In Spanish, AYA-Expanse-8B joins the top three for QA, EuroLLM-9B for reasoning, and RigoChat-7B is in the top four for language proficiency.
In Catalan, EuroLLM ranks among the top three for both QA and reasoning tasks.
For Basque, Salamandra-7B-IT is the second-best QA model, while Latxa-7B and Salamandra-7B occupy the first and second positions in reasoning and the third and second positions in classification, respectively.
In Galician, EuroLLM-9B is the best model for QA, followed by its instructed version, Salamandra-7B ranks third in reasoning, and AYA-Expanse-8B takes second place in NLI.

Report issue for preceding element

##### Performance by training data configuration

Report issue for preceding element

It is valuable to compare the different language configuration strategies in training.
Salamandra and EuroLLM, by
distributing tokens in the pre-training data fairly among languages, achieve homogeneous performance and, in particular, reinforce Galician and Basque, but lose ground in Spanish and Catalan to models supported by high-resource corpora.
Gemma2, which prioritizes volume over linguistic diversity, stands out for just the opposite; training on a large but linguistically imbalanced dataset allows the model to transfer patterns learned from English, maths, and code, and consistently rank among the top models overall.
This shows that, sometimes, breadth of knowledge can compensate for the lack of language-specific data.

Report issue for preceding element

The results confirm that the strategy of pre-training from scratch on a large multilingual corpus is the one that offers the most consistent and homogeneous coverage. Qwen-2.5, trained on 29 languages, and Llama-3.1, trained on 8, rank high in all languages.
Moreover, systems that use continuous pre-training - adding large-scale data in a new language plus some English data to avoid catastrophic forgetting - achieve peak scores in the target language; e.g., Latxa holds the second-highest mark in Basque reasoning.
Finally, models that just fine-tune on target language data without extending the pre-training (e.g., RigoChat or some Instruct variants) gain fluency and style, but the improvement in reasoning and QA tasks is modest, and models rarely enter the top 10.
In summary, the earlier and deeper the model is exposed to the target languages, the higher its average scores; a posteriori strategies function as beneficial reinforcers, especially in less-resourced languages, but do not replace the power of extensive multilingual pre-training.

Report issue for preceding element

##### Performance by training compute

Report issue for preceding element

Regarding the computational budget and the hardware used, public data is scarce.
Regarding large tech companies we can consider Llama-3.1-8B, which was trained for 1.5M GPU-h. By contrast, other evaluated models required three to four orders of magnitude fewer. As expected, the results confirm that teams with access to GPUs/TPUs and high-end accelerators (TPUv5p, H100 or A100 in large clusters) can apply the strategies that we highlighted in the previous section as the most successful - massive multilingual pre-training and continuous pre-training - reflecting in significantly higher average scores. However, the same results also nuance the linear relationship between investment and performance
as Salamandra-7B, despite its large budget (600 k GPU-h), falls in the middle of the table. Overall, the dashboard illustrates that computational abundance enables impactful techniques, but that dataset quality and fine-tuning remain decisive levers for converting that power into real performance.

Report issue for preceding element

##### Performance vs. size

Report issue for preceding element

In general, our experiments show some correlation between performance and size, with models in the range of 1-2B parameters achieving better scores for their size. This is particularly true for Gemma-2-2B and Qwen-2.5-1.5B, both base and instructed models.
Among the top 10 models, we find that all have between 8 and 9 billion parameters, except for the quantized versions from the Qwen family.

Report issue for preceding element

##### Performance per model type

Report issue for preceding element

For the same VRAM requirement, quantized models with more parameters outperform full-precision models with fewer parameters.
We don’t observe any correlation between performance and whether the model is pre-trained or instruction-tuned, as this varies depending on the model.

### 4.2 Energy consumption

Report issue for preceding element

The total computational resources amount to 660.87 hours of processing time and 582.84 kWh of energy consumption, resulting in 92.09 kg of CO2 emissions.
On average, each model consumes 9.25 kWh (median 6.88, SD 8.42), showing a wide variety in energy usage.
The models that consume the most energy are Grommeanuer-7B-IT, Qwen-2.5-32B-IT-GPTQ-Int4, and Qwen-2.5-14B-IT-GPTQ-Int8, each exceeding 30 kWh. On the other hand, Salamandra-2b, FLOR-1.3B-IT, and LLama-3.2-1B-IT are the most energy-efficient, consuming less than 2.1 kWh each.

Report issue for preceding element

##### Energy consumption vs. size

Report issue for preceding element

As expected, a strong correlation between model size and energy dissipation is observed, as the number of arithmetic operations required to predict a token is related to the number of parameters of the model.
However, some outliers are observed, such as Qwen, which consumes significantly more energy across all its sizes compared to other models. Conversely, models like FLOR exhibit considerably lower energy consumption across their different sizes relative to other models of similar scale.

Report issue for preceding element

##### Energy consumption vs. task

Report issue for preceding element

Similarly, as anticipated, text generation tasks such as summarization require more energy for evaluation.
Since LLMs generate text token by token and their prediction speed remains constant (assuming the same hardware and stable conditions), the most energy-intensive tasks are expected to be those that require the generation of larger amounts of text.

Report issue for preceding element

##### Energy consumption vs. performance

Report issue for preceding element

Our experiments show a strong correlation between the energy consumed at inference and the model performance. For one of the overall top models, Gemma-2-9B, its instruction-tuned version excels with a third of the energy consumed by the base version. We observe a trend of instructed models consuming less energy, due to the verbosity of base models.

## 5 Conclusions and Future Work

Report issue for preceding element

In this paper, we propose a methodology to create community-driven leaderboards, including
key points to gather diverse datasets and the rationale behind a more efficient and accessible evaluation setup. In doing so, we hope to inspire the creation of more leaderboards that fulfil the needs of diverse linguistic communities.

Report issue for preceding element

In particular, we present La Leaderboard, the first open-source leaderboard to evaluate LLMs in languages from Spain and Latin America. It is the result of a collaboration among 13 research groups.
La Leaderboardconsists of 66 datasets in Spanish, Catalan, Basque, and Galician, and covers a wide range of task types and domains.
The results of evaluating 50 LLMs suggest that the top-performing models in the target languages are Gemma-2-9B base and instruct, Llama-3.1-8B-IT, and the quantized versions of Qwen-2.5-IT 14B and 32B. However, for domain-specific applications, particular linguistic contexts, or deployment scenarios with computational constraints or transparency requirements, alternative models (e.g., Salamandra-7B and EuroLLM-9B) demonstrate competitive performance metrics.

Report issue for preceding element

Our planned next steps include evaluating the recently donated datasets, with a special focus on indigenous languages. We will also add larger open models and proprietary models.
Moreover, we are organizing a hackathon to create a benchmark to measure cultural adequacy in each Spanish-speaking country.
Finally, we welcome any person or organization interested in joining our effort.
This way, we hope that La Leaderboardwill keep evolving to include more languages, language varieties, and use cases that motivate the development of LLMs that better serve our diverse community.

Report issue for preceding element

## Limitations

Report issue for preceding element

##### Indigenous languages

Report issue for preceding element

We acknowledge that indigenous languages from Latin America are not yet included among the evaluation results of La Leaderboard.
However, we have ongoing collaborations to include existing benchmarks and create new ones to keep extending La Leaderboardto be as inclusive as possible and reflect the diversity of the Spanish-speaking community.

Report issue for preceding element

##### Spanish language varieties

Report issue for preceding element

Currently, the leaderboard includes datasets in the Spanish varieties of Spain, Mexico, Argentina, Chile, and Uruguay. Although we don’t know the exact origin of all the samples from some third-party datasets, we estimate that less than 25% of all the Spanish datasets in the leaderboard come from LATAM. We plan to increase this percentage by collaborating with LATAM research groups in the creation of an open hackathon.

Report issue for preceding element

##### Large and proprietary models

Report issue for preceding element

To improve the coverage of the state-of-the-art language models for the use cases included in La Leaderboard, it would be interesting to evaluate larger language models
as well as proprietary models.

Report issue for preceding element

##### Contamination

Report issue for preceding element

Another pending task is to analyse potential contamination Sainz et al. ( [2023](https://arxiv.org/html/2507.00999v1#bib.bib91 "")) within our leaderboard. We have not addressed this yet because a high percentage of the datasets used are very recent and niche, making it unlikely that they have been incorporated into training data, unlike more established benchmarks such as MMLU Hendrycks et al. ( [2021a](https://arxiv.org/html/2507.00999v1#bib.bib44 "")); Wang et al. ( [2024b](https://arxiv.org/html/2507.00999v1#bib.bib104 "")); Taghanaki et al. ( [2024](https://arxiv.org/html/2507.00999v1#bib.bib100 "")) that serve as primary pillars in model evaluation in every model report. Nevertheless, we have started to evaluate contamination to ensure in the short-term future that we provide high-quality results.

Report issue for preceding element

For the datasets specifically created for La Leaderboard, we advised the corresponding authors to release them gated to avoid being unintentionally included in training datasets by web scraping; AQuAS and RagQuAS are gated. The authors of TELEIA decided to release an adaptation of their dataset and keep the original private to be able to analyze contamination through time.

## Ethical Considerations

Report issue for preceding element

##### Fair representation

Report issue for preceding element

Since our objective is to establish an evaluation standard for Latin America and Spain, it is important to properly represent the linguistic and cultural diversity of the community in order to avoid the perpetuation, or even amplification, of stereotypes and inequalities.

Report issue for preceding element

##### Third-party datasets

Report issue for preceding element

Some of the evaluation datasets included in La Leaderboardwere created by organizations other than our data contributors.
As a result, we acknowledge the possibility that some of these datasets may have been developed using practices that could be considered unethical. These concerns range from potential legal violations to extractive data collection methods that may impact disadvantaged communities.

Report issue for preceding element

##### Environmental impact

Report issue for preceding element

Evaluating 50 language models on 66 tasks required 660.87 hours of compute, translating to 92.09 kg of CO2. However, we hope that by publishing a comprehensive evaluation of the available models, La Leaderboardwill contribute to reducing the total environmental impact of individual private evaluations.

Report issue for preceding element

##### Misuse of La Leaderboard

Report issue for preceding element

We welcome model submissions from everyone. This could potentially lead to overuse, with people sending many different versions of the same model. We plan to mitigate this behaviour by following the spam mitigation strategies from the Open LLM Leaderboard Fourrier et al. ( [2024](https://arxiv.org/html/2507.00999v1#bib.bib34 "")).

## AQuAS

Report issue for preceding element

The Abstractive Question-Answering in Spanish (AQuAS) dataset (Instituto de Ingeniería del Conocimiento, [2024a](https://arxiv.org/html/2507.00999v1#bib.bib48 "")),
developed by Instituto de Ingeniería del Conocimiento, is a monolingual Spanish dataset designed for abstractive question-answering. It contains 107 examples covering a diverse range of topics, including finance, insurance, healthcare, music, and law.
Each example consists of a context passage, a related question, and a human-crafted answer.
The dataset is aimed at evaluating the ability of large language models (LLMs) to generate well-formed, coherent, and informative responses.

Fabbri, Diego Mares, Jorge Flores, Meher Mankikar, Ernesto Hernandez, Dean Lee, Bing Liu, Chen Xing Scale AI Report issue for preceding element ###### Résumé Report issue for preceding element Although recent Large Language Models (LLMs) have shown rapid improvement on reasoning benchmarks in English, the evaluation of such LLMs’ multilingual reasoning capability across diverse languages and cultural contexts remains limited. Existing multilingual reasoning benchmarks are typically constructed by translating existing English reasoning benchmarks, biasing these benchmarks towards reasoning problems with context in English language/cultures. In this work, we introduce the Multilingual Native Reasoning Challenge (MultiNRC), a benchmark designed to assess LLMs on more than 1,000 native, linguistic and culturally grounded reasoning questions written by native speakers in French, Spanish, and Chinese. MultiNRC covers four core reasoning categories: language-specific linguistic reasoning, wordplay & riddles, cultural/tradition reasoning, and math reasoning with cultural relevance. For cultural/tradition reasoning and math reasoning with cultural relevance, we also provide English equivalent translations of the multilingual questions by manual translation from native speakers fluent in English. This set of English equivalents can provide a direct comparison of LLM reasoning capacity in other languages vs. English on the same reasoning questions. We systematically evaluate current 14 leading LLMs covering most LLM families on MultiNRC and its English equivalent set. The results show that (1) current LLMs are still not good at native multilingual reasoning, with none scoring above 50% on MultiNRC; (2) LLMs exhibit distinct strengths and weaknesses in handling linguistic, cultural, and logical reasoning tasks; (3) Most models perform substantially better in math reasoning in English compared to in original languages (+10%), indicating persistent challenges with culturally grounded knowledge. Report issue for preceding element ## 1 Introduction Report issue for preceding element Enhancing the reasoning capabilities of Large Language Models (LLMs) is a critical area of ongoing research and development (OpenAI, [2024](https://arxiv.org/html/2507.17476v1#bib.bib19 ""); Guo et al., [2025](https://arxiv.org/html/2507.17476v1#bib.bib10 "")). Consequently, thorough and diverse reasoning evaluation benchmarks in English have been developed to assess LLMs’ improved reasoning capabilities. These evaluation datasets cover a variety of reasoning tasks, including commonsense reasoning (Zellers et al., [2019](https://arxiv.org/html/2507.17476v1#bib.bib32 ""); Sakaguchi et al., [2020](https://arxiv.org/html/2507.17476v1#bib.bib25 ""); Clark et al., [2018](https://arxiv.org/html/2507.17476v1#bib.bib4 "")), language-understanding reasoning in English (Hendrycks et al., [2021](https://arxiv.org/html/2507.17476v1#bib.bib13 ""); Wang et al., [2024b](https://arxiv.org/html/2507.17476v1#bib.bib29 "")), STEM reasoning (Cobbe et al., [2021](https://arxiv.org/html/2507.17476v1#bib.bib5 ""); Zhong et al., [2024](https://arxiv.org/html/2507.17476v1#bib.bib34 ""); [Hendrycks et al.,](https://arxiv.org/html/2507.17476v1#bib.bib12 "")), and logical reasoning (Liu et al., [2020](https://arxiv.org/html/2507.17476v1#bib.bib17 ""); Yu et al., [2020](https://arxiv.org/html/2507.17476v1#bib.bib31 ""); Geva et al., [2021](https://arxiv.org/html/2507.17476v1#bib.bib9 "")). These benchmarks play a critical role in guiding the evolution of the reasoning capacity of LLMs. Report issue for preceding element While a large number of these benchmarks have been developed in English, the landscape of multilingual reasoning benchmarks is less developed, comprehensive, and equitable. Existing multilingual reasoning benchmarks are largely created by translating existing English reasoning benchmarks (automatically, manually, or hybrid) into target languages (Shi et al., [2023](https://arxiv.org/html/2507.17476v1#bib.bib27 ""); Patel et al., [2021](https://arxiv.org/html/2507.17476v1#bib.bib22 "")). Benchmarks created by directly translating English-centric content may reflect the cultural framing and linguistic characteristic of English, which are not globally representative. As a result, reasoning tasks that require native linguistic or cultural understanding are often missing, leaving gaps in the evaluation of non-English language reasoning abilities. Consequently, we are still largely unaware of how state-of-the-art (SOTA) LLMs perform on genuinely native multilingual reasoning tasks that demand both linguistic diversity and cultural or contextual depth. Report issue for preceding element Motivated by this gap, we develop the Multilingual Native Reasoning Challenge (MultiNRC), a new multilingual evaluation benchmark that contains native and challenging reasoning questions of the targeted language, to assess LLMs’ reasoning capability under a natural and native context. Specifically, MultiNRC contains four categories of reasoning questions: language-specific linguistic reasoning, wordplay riddles, cultural/tradition reasoning, and finally mathematical reasoning with cultural relevance. We first release MultiNRC in French, Spanish, and Chinese; Table [1](https://arxiv.org/html/2507.17476v1#S1.T1 "Table 1 ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ MultiNRC: A Challenging and Native Multilingual Reasoning Evaluation Benchmark for LLMs") shows examples of the four categories in different languages. To build MultiNRC, we recruit native speakers of each language to create challenging reasoning questions and ground-truth final answers according to the definitions of the four categories above. We only accept reasoning questions that cause at least 3333 out of 5555 SOTA LLMs to fail, and we facilitate MultiNRC with automatic evaluation with LLM-as-a-judge, for fast and accurate model assessments. Automatic evaluation is made possible by only including reasoning questions with an objective and short ground-truth final answer; we find that our automatic evaluation has more than 95% alignment with human judgment on MultiNRC. Report issue for preceding element We thoroughly evaluate current SOTA LLMs on MultiNRC. We find that the best performing LLM, o3-pro (OpenAI, [2025](https://arxiv.org/html/2507.17476v1#bib.bib21 "")) released in April 2025, achieves only 49% accuracy according to automatic evaluation with respect to our ground-truth final answers, indicating the high difficulty level of MultiNRC for SOTA models. We find that o3 variants along with Gemini-2.5-Pro (June 2025) (Comanici et al., [2025](https://arxiv.org/html/2507.17476v1#bib.bib6 "")) greatly outperform other models, and that LLMs also rank differently across MultiNRC reasoning categories, suggesting that the taxonomy of MultiNRC provides a more informative view to guide LLM performance improvement. For example, Gemini-2.5-Pro ranks third on average accuracy among models but ranks first in math reasoning with cultural relevance. A wide range of benchmarks have been developed to evaluate the reasoning capabilities of LLMs across commonsense, logical, and STEM reasoning domains. Commonsense reasoning benchmarks aim to evaluate an LLM’s ability to apply everyday knowledge and logical inference to understand and interact with the world in a human-like way. HellaSwag (Zellers et al., [2019](https://arxiv.org/html/2507.17476v1#bib.bib32 "")) and WinoGrande (Sakaguchi et al., [2020](https://arxiv.org/html/2507.17476v1#bib.bib25 "")) are two widely-adopted examples. Logical and deductive reasoning benchmarks, such as ReClor (Yu et al., [2020](https://arxiv.org/html/2507.17476v1#bib.bib31 "")) and StrategyQA (Geva et al., [2021](https://arxiv.org/html/2507.17476v1#bib.bib9 "")), and ARC-AGI (Chollet et al., [2024](https://arxiv.org/html/2507.17476v1#bib.bib3 "")), are designed to evaluate an LLM’s capacity to apply formal rules of logic and to perform deductive, inductive, or abductive inference given a set of premises. To comprehensively assess both general knowledge and reasoning, multitask benchmarks like MMLU-Pro (Wang et al., [2024b](https://arxiv.org/html/2507.17476v1#bib.bib29 "")) have emerged, expanding on prior efforts in MMLU (Hendrycks et al., [2021](https://arxiv.org/html/2507.17476v1#bib.bib13 "")) by including more rigorous reasoning components and a broader coverage of academic subjects, rather than just factual recall. STEM and math reasoning benchmarks, such as AIME (Mathematical Association of America, [2024](https://arxiv.org/html/2507.17476v1#bib.bib18 "")) and MATH ( [Hendrycks et al.,](https://arxiv.org/html/2507.17476v1#bib.bib12 "")), are specifically designed to assess an LLM’s proficiency in solving complex, multi-step mathematical problems. Distinct from prior benchmarks, we focus on evaluating reasoning over linguistic, wordplay, cultural/tradition, and math questions, each written by native speakers to capture local language and cultural nuance. Report issue for preceding element Multilingual reasoning benchmarks. Compared to LLM reasoning evaluation in English, multilingual reasoning benchmarks are less developed. A majority of them are translated from existing English reasoning benchmarks (Li et al., [2024](https://arxiv.org/html/2507.17476v1#bib.bib16 ""); Shi et al., [2023](https://arxiv.org/html/2507.17476v1#bib.bib27 ""); Huang et al., [2025](https://arxiv.org/html/2507.17476v1#bib.bib14 "")). Among them, MMLU-ProX (Xuan et al., [2025](https://arxiv.org/html/2507.17476v1#bib.bib30 "")), is built by translating the existing English benchmark, MMLU-Pro (Wang et al., [2024b](https://arxiv.org/html/2507.17476v1#bib.bib29 "")), to evaluate advanced reasoning across multiple languages. The initial translation of the English questions into the other 28 languages was performed using multiple LLMs, followed by an expert review phase. Similarly, MGSM (Shi et al., [2023](https://arxiv.org/html/2507.17476v1#bib.bib27 "")) and BenchMAX (Huang et al., [2025](https://arxiv.org/html/2507.17476v1#bib.bib14 "")) are translated from GSM8K  (Cobbe et al., [2021](https://arxiv.org/html/2507.17476v1#bib.bib5 "")) and GPQA ( [Rein et al.,](https://arxiv.org/html/2507.17476v1#bib.bib24 "")). BenchMAX is built with an initial machine translation and a meticulous post-editing process in which each sample was independently reviewed by three distinct native-language annotators. MGSM was created by manually translating 250 problems selected from the English GSM8K dataset. An approach to avoid translating existing English benchmarks is by using exam questions in non-English languages (Hardalov et al., [2020](https://arxiv.org/html/2507.17476v1#bib.bib11 ""); Zhang et al., [2023](https://arxiv.org/html/2507.17476v1#bib.bib33 ""); Wang et al., [2024a](https://arxiv.org/html/2507.17476v1#bib.bib28 "")). However, such benchmarks, with M3Exam as an example, have mostly multichoice questions that assess knowledge instead of reasoning and are too easy for SOTA models, as suggested by their reported GPT-4 results in 2023 (Zhang et al., [2023](https://arxiv.org/html/2507.17476v1#bib.bib33 "")). Another example of data collected from native languages is MultiLoko Hupkes & Bogoychev ( [2025](https://arxiv.org/html/2507.17476v1#bib.bib15 "")), which collects SQuAD-style Rajpurkar et al. ( [2016](https://arxiv.org/html/2507.17476v1#bib.bib23 "")) questions from the most popular Wikipedia pages for each language, rated for their local relevance to the language. While this work also analyzes model performance on English equivalents, the focus of our work is on reasoning questions over linguistic and cultural knowledge and nuance, and not just factual knowledge. Report issue for preceding element ## 3 Evaluation Benchmark Overview Report issue for preceding element Below we describe the Multilingual Native Reasoning Challenge (MultiNRC) benchmark, detailing our choice of reasoning categories, English equivalent set of multilingual prompts, as well as dataset construction methodology and statistics. Report issue for preceding element ### 3.1 Reasoning Categories Report issue for preceding element MultiNRC contains 4444 categories of reasoning questions. They are language-specific linguistic reasoning, wordplay riddles, cultural/tradition reasoning, and finally, math reasoning with cultural relevance. We extract and summarize the 4444 categories from preliminary crowd-sourced native and challenging reasoning questions that we collect for multiple languages and cultures. The 4444 categories are uniquely defined from each other to assess the different capabilities of LLM required in multilingual reasoning tasks. Table [1](https://arxiv.org/html/2507.17476v1#S1.T1 "Table 1 ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ MultiNRC: A Challenging and Native Multilingual Reasoning Evaluation Benchmark for LLMs") shows example tasks in all categories, which are described in the following paragraphs. Additional examples can be found in the Appendix in Table [7](https://arxiv.org/html/2507.17476v1#A1.T7 "Table 7 ‣ Machine Translation and English Reasoning ‣ A.2 Additional Evaluation Results ‣ Annexe A Appendix ‣ MultiNRC: A Challenging and Native Multilingual Reasoning Evaluation Benchmark for LLMs"). Such questions require reasoning about language structure or usage. Examples under this category include word formation problems, relation inference based on language conventions, etc. We enforce that the questions should require multi-step reasoning, instead of mere linguistic feature identification without reasoning. In the French example in Table [1](https://arxiv.org/html/2507.17476v1#S1.T1 "Table 1 ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ MultiNRC: A Challenging and Native Multilingual Reasoning Evaluation Benchmark for LLMs"), the question requires recognizing that the noun délice is masculine in the singular and feminine in the plural, an uncommon grammatical characteristic not present in English. Report issue for preceding element Wordplay & Riddles contain puzzles that rely on the clever and ambiguous use of the target language, often involving multiple meanings, homophones, or puns. Since such reasoning questions usually use very language-specific homophones or puns, there are no English translations that can provide the exact meaning of such questions. Our evaluations later show that this category is one of the most difficult for LLMs. In the Chinese example shown in Table [1](https://arxiv.org/html/2507.17476v1#S1.T1 "Table 1 ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ MultiNRC: A Challenging and Native Multilingual Reasoning Evaluation Benchmark for LLMs"), the question requires the respondent to use a Chengyu (Ancient Chinese idiom) involving a pun or homophone as an answer to a playful riddle, thus demanding clever reasoning. Report issue for preceding element Cultural/Tradition Reasoning questions require reasoning through timelines, behaviors, or customs derived from local traditions, holidays, or ceremonies. Similar to other categories, we enforce the assessment of LLM reasoning capabilities and exclude purely factual questions. In the Spanish example in the table, the question requires identifying the date of a local holiday (Día de la Candelaria) and reasoning about travel dates to ensure two full weekends are spent at the destination, demonstrating an understanding of local traditions and applying multi-step temporal reasoning. Report issue for preceding element Math Reasoning with Cultural Relevance questions involve calculations based on cultural-specific counting systems, calendars, currencies, or numerical phrasing. As above, it must require at least 1 reasoning step based on a culturally specific element, and we do not allow pure arithmetic or logic without cultural grounding. In the French example in the table, the question requires the application of culturally specific knowledge about the ’viager’ real estate system and historical events (such as the date of the Cannes Film Festival) to determine the financial break-even point for a property purchase, thereby testing mathematical reasoning within a local context. Report issue for preceding element ### 3.2 English Equivalent Prompts Report issue for preceding element In order to test the reasoning gap in English vs. non-English languages, we further ask annotators to translate the native prompts and ground-truth final answers into English. Annotators judge the validity of machine-translated prompts from 5 SOTA models and choose the most relevant machine-translated prompt from the above pipeline as a base for translation, or translate from scratch as needed. Our annotators focus on translating the logic, not literal words, ensuring that the English translation is also culturally grounded and requires similar reasoning. We only produce English translations for the Cultural/Tradition Reasoning and Math Reasoning categories. The translated English version retains the structure and solvability of the original, with the translator trying to translate cultural or linguistic characteristics into English. Examples of English translated prompts and answers are shown in the Appendix in Table [8](https://arxiv.org/html/2507.17476v1#A1.T8 "Table 8 ‣ Machine Translation and English Reasoning ‣ A.2 Additional Evaluation Results ‣ Annexe A Appendix ‣ MultiNRC: A Challenging and Native Multilingual Reasoning Evaluation Benchmark for LLMs"). We found that the categories of Language-specific Linguistic Reasoning and Wordplay & Riddles could not be reliably translated into English, as they often rely on linguistic phenomena that do not translate or exist in English. Thus, we exclude these categories from the English equivalent set. Report issue for preceding element ### 3.3 Data Collection/Review and Statistics Report issue for preceding element To collect data for MultiNRC, native speakers start by writing reasoning prompts according to the definition of one of the four categories mentioned above. For each prompt, the annotator also writes a ground-truth final answer (GTFA), consisting of either a single word or a short phrase/sentence. We then pull model responses from five top models at the time of creation across model providers: Google’s Gemini-2.5-pro (Comanici et al., [2025](https://arxiv.org/html/2507.17476v1#bib.bib6 "")), o4-mini (OpenAI, [2025](https://arxiv.org/html/2507.17476v1#bib.bib21 "")), Claude 3.7-Sonnet (Anthropic, [2025](https://arxiv.org/html/2507.17476v1#bib.bib2 "")), Deepseek R1 (DeepSeek-AI, [2025](https://arxiv.org/html/2507.17476v1#bib.bib8 "")), and Llama-4 Maverick (AI, [2024](https://arxiv.org/html/2507.17476v1#bib.bib1 "")). The 5 model responses are presented to annotators in a random order. We only keep the reasoning questions that 3 or more of the 5 models fail to correctly answer. Report issue for preceding element After the raw data is collected, we have two native-speaker reviewer layers to assess the quality of the data from different aspects. The first native-speaker reviewer layer is to assess the quality of the prompt and GTFA pairs. At this layer we would assess both the GTFA’s accuracy and the prompt’s reasonableness and alignment with category definition. The second native-speaker reviewer layer assesses whether there are truly 3 out of 5 SOTA model failures, given the verified prompt and GTFA pairs. This is to verify the difficulty level of the collected data. We show the statistics of the final dataset after these collection/review steps in Table [2](https://arxiv.org/html/2507.17476v1#S3.T2 "Table 2 ‣ 3.1 Reasoning Categories ‣ 3 Evaluation Benchmark Overview ‣ MultiNRC: A Challenging and Native Multilingual Reasoning Evaluation Benchmark for LLMs"). We collect roughly the same amount of examples across categories and languages, more than the 250 per-language count of the popular MGSM dataset (Shi et al., [2023](https://arxiv.org/html/2507.17476v1#bib.bib27 "")). We also annotate subcategories of the cultural and linguistic nuances present in the prompts. The results of this analysis are found in the Appendix in Table [9](https://arxiv.org/html/2507.17476v1#A1.T9 "Table 9 ‣ Machine Translation and English Reasoning ‣ A.2 Additional Evaluation Results ‣ Annexe A Appendix ‣ MultiNRC: A Challenging and Native Multilingual Reasoning Evaluation Benchmark for LLMs"). Report issue for preceding element ## 4 Experimental Settings Report issue for preceding element #### Reasoning Settings Report issue for preceding element We perform experiments in the following settings: 1) Original in which the model is given the original multilingual question, and prompted to provide an explanation and a short final answer in the native language of the question. 2) En in which the model answers human-translated English equivalent questions (illustrated in Section 3.2) in English. By comparing En vs Original, we can see the difference in model’s abilities to understand and reason about local linguistic and cultural nuance in the local language versus English. Hupkes & Bogoychev ( [2025](https://arxiv.org/html/2507.17476v1#bib.bib15 "")) refer to this as the Mother Tongue Effect. 3) EnT/R in which the model is prompted to produce an English translation of the native prompt by itself, reason/explain in English and return the native final answer. 4) EnR in which the model is asked to reason in English on the native prompt and return the native language response. The results of these last two settings are found in Appendix [A.2](https://arxiv.org/html/2507.17476v1#A1.SS2 "A.2 Additional Evaluation Results ‣ Annexe A Appendix ‣ MultiNRC: A Challenging and Native Multilingual Reasoning Evaluation Benchmark for LLMs"). Report issue for preceding element #### Automatic Evaluation Report issue for preceding element As described above, we collect human judgment of the correctness of model responses for 5 SOTA models on our benchmark. In order to scale annotations, we leverage an LLM judge that takes the prompt, GTFA, and model response and produces a correct/not correct judgment as well as reasoning behind the judgment. We found that GPT-4.1(OpenAI, [2024](https://arxiv.org/html/2507.17476v1#bib.bib20 "")) as the judge results in an over 95% agreement with our human judgments and a Scott’s Pi (Scott, [1955](https://arxiv.org/html/2507.17476v1#bib.bib26 "")) of 0.88, indicating strong reliability of our metric, and thus we utilize this automatic judge for all reported results. Note that all experimental results use pass@1. Report issue for preceding element #### Model Selection and Inference Parameters Report issue for preceding element We select 14 model variations across model providers, to obtain as generalizable results as possible given current SOTA models. We test a range of recent LLMs including Google’s Gemini-2.5-pro DeepMind ( [2025](https://arxiv.org/html/2507.17476v1#bib.bib7 "")), OpenAI’s o3 and o4-mini OpenAI ( [2025](https://arxiv.org/html/2507.17476v1#bib.bib21 "")), gpt-4.1 OpenAI ( [2024](https://arxiv.org/html/2507.17476v1#bib.bib20 "")), Anthropic’s Claude (Opus, Sonnet, including thinking and non-thinking models), and Llama-4 AI ( [2024](https://arxiv.org/html/2507.17476v1#bib.bib1 "")). Note that -high or -medium refers to the reasoning effort setting. We generate with max completion tokens of 32k, thinking budget of 16k where applicable, and default to the model provider’s default temperature. Positive values indicate a performance improvement on English translated queries vs Original.Report issue for preceding element ## 5 Results and Analysis Report issue for preceding element The main results on MultiNRC are found in Table [3](https://arxiv.org/html/2507.17476v1#S4.T3 "Table 3 ‣ Model Selection and Inference Parameters ‣ 4 Experimental Settings ‣ MultiNRC: A Challenging and Native Multilingual Reasoning Evaluation Benchmark for LLMs"), showing model performance in the Original setting, along with 95% confidence intervals. We note that o3 variants along with Gemini-2.5-pro-preview-06-05 score clearly better than any other model. However, no model surpasses 50% accuracy on the dataset, underscoring the difficulty of MultiNRC and the substantial performance gaps even among top models. We also find trends of progress in recent models; for example, Deepseek-R1-0528 improves considerably over the initial Deepseek-R1, and GPT-4.1 outperforms GPT-4o. Furthermore, thinking model variants (e.g., Claude-4-Opus-20250514-thinking) consistently show better performance within the same family, indicating the benefit of enhanced reasoning effort. Report issue for preceding element In Table [4](https://arxiv.org/html/2507.17476v1#S4.T4 "Table 4 ‣ Model Selection and Inference Parameters ‣ 4 Experimental Settings ‣ MultiNRC: A Challenging and Native Multilingual Reasoning Evaluation Benchmark for LLMs"), we break down model performance on MultiNRC in the Original setting by both category and language. Math reasoning questions are the most challenging overall, with an average accuracy of just 23.3% across all questions, and especially low scores in Spanish. In contrast, linguistic and cultural reasoning tasks see higher scores, with average accuracies of 34.8% and 31.1%. Wordplay remains a consistently difficult category for all languages, although the models score better in French for this category. Spanish stands out as the most challenging language across categories, particularly for math and wordplay. Some models exhibit distinct strengths in particular languages and categories, as seen in Deepseek-R1-05-28’s higher rank on Chinese Math and Linguistic categories. These results illustrate that model performance is affected not only by the reasoning category itself but also by the interaction between languages and reasoning categories. In Appendix [A.2](https://arxiv.org/html/2507.17476v1#A1.SS2 "A.2 Additional Evaluation Results ‣ Annexe A Appendix ‣ MultiNRC: A Challenging and Native Multilingual Reasoning Evaluation Benchmark for LLMs"), we provide an additional comparison of the gap between the top and worst performing language for each model. Report issue for preceding element Within categories, we see large performance gaps between models. For example, although top-performing models generally struggle on Math overall, Gemini performs much better than others due to its strong results in Spanish Math questions. Similarly, o3-pro demonstrates a significant improvement in Wordplay, especially French Wordplay (75.9%). As a result, models often rank differently across MultiNRC reasoning categories and languages. These results suggest that the taxonomy of MultiNRC provides a more informative view to guide LLM performance improvements. Report issue for preceding element The results described above show a full picture of LLM performance in Original setting of MultiNRC. Table [5](https://arxiv.org/html/2507.17476v1#S4.T5 "Table 5 ‣ Model Selection and Inference Parameters ‣ 4 Experimental Settings ‣ MultiNRC: A Challenging and Native Multilingual Reasoning Evaluation Benchmark for LLMs") presents the performance delta, calculated as the difference between accuracy on English-translated questions and the original native questions, for both Cultural and Math tasks across French, Spanish, and Chinese. We observe that scores on English-translated versions of Chinese and Spanish questions are often higher than the original scores, although this is model-dependent, and several top-performing models, such as o3 variants, perform better in French compared to Original. These results suggest that for certain languages and categories, language-specific strengths and weaknesses remain a significant factor in LLM performance. Report issue for preceding element For math reasoning, we observe a substantial improvement when models are given English equivalents, with especially pronounced gains for Spanish (+19.1) and Chinese (+12.5). Our case studies highlight that LLMs are able to surface the correct background knowledge and relevant values more reliably for the math problems presented in English, leading to higher accuracy on these tasks. In contrast, for cultural reasoning, the difference is negligible on average. This suggests that while translation to English can unlock knowledge for certain tasks such as math reasoning questions, performance improvement on culturally grounded tasks remains limited, likely due to the lack of exposure of the models to specific cultural knowledge, regardless of language. We present case studies of examples where o3 answers English equivalents correctly but provides incorrect answers to the original questions in Appendix [A.2](https://arxiv.org/html/2507.17476v1#A1.SS2 "A.2 Additional Evaluation Results ‣ Annexe A Appendix ‣ MultiNRC: A Challenging and Native Multilingual Reasoning Evaluation Benchmark for LLMs"), along with more quantified analysis on model discrepancies and consistency. We observe that 66% of the problems are either solved correctly or incorrectly by both models. Among the problems that the two models perform differently on, our error analysis suggests that o3 performs better on French Wordplay examples, where Gemini is more likely to miss cultural nuance or wordplay (yielding literal or surface-level responses). However, Gemini performs better on Chinese cultural prompts. The Spanish example in Table [6](https://arxiv.org/html/2507.17476v1#S5.T6 "Table 6 ‣ 5 Results and Analysis ‣ MultiNRC: A Challenging and Native Multilingual Reasoning Evaluation Benchmark for LLMs") is an example in which both models fail. Both models used incorrect values for the codo de ribera unit, leading to a difference in calculating the number of porrones required. In the French example shown, Gemini fails to recognize the homophonic pun between ”marre tôt” and ”marteau,” while o3 correctly identifies and explains this wordplay. In the Chinese example, o3 undercounts the days between festivals by one. Report issue for preceding element These case studies highlight the sensitivity of large language models to linguistic and cultural nuances, especially when reasoning in languages other than English. In our work, we do not explore models designed or finetuned specifically to be multilingual, and we leave an evaluation of these models on the benchmark for future work. We selected French, Spanish, and Chinese as initial languages given the large number of global speakers and the authors’ familiarity with these languages. To draw wider conclusions about multilingual performance, it will be be important to include additional languages in future work. We expect that extending this benchmark to low-resource languages would magnify the struggle of current models in dealing with local knowledge, linguistic phenomena, and complex reasoning. Furthermore, our analysis does not explicitly consider the effect of regional or dialectal variation, which is present in languages like Spanish and Chinese, and future work could examine how these differences impact model performance. This underscores the need for both more diverse training data and tailored model evaluation to ensure robust, equitable progress in multilingual LLMs. Report issue for preceding element ## 7 Conclusion Report issue for preceding element We introduce MultiNRC, a challenging benchmark designed to evaluate the multilingual abilities of LLMs through linguistically and culturally-nuanced reasoning questions. By constructing diverse native reasoning questions in French, Spanish, and Chinese, we highlight ongoing challenges for LLMs when faced with linguistically and culturally nuanced reasoning tasks across multiple languages. Our evaluation shows that while English translation can boost performance on some tasks, substantial gaps remain for many culturally and linguistically nuanced questions. We hope that MultiNRC will serve as a robust testbed for future advances in multilingual LLM development, and we release our dataset to further research in this direction. For example, one French cultural question requires knowledge of both local festivals and the French calendar of saints. The French wordplay question relies on recognizing that ”mon chien Michel” is a homophone for ”Mont Saint-Michel,” combining everyday language with a cultural reference. Report issue for preceding element We also include English-equivalent prompts in Table [8](https://arxiv.org/html/2507.17476v1#A1.T8 "Table 8 ‣ Machine Translation and English Reasoning ‣ A.2 Additional Evaluation Results ‣ Annexe A Appendix ‣ MultiNRC: A Challenging and Native Multilingual Reasoning Evaluation Benchmark for LLMs"). For example, the French mathematical question asks for the difference in height between Paris’s iconic monument and the tallest residential tower in the country, which are translated from French while keeping the logic and required knowledge for the question intact. Report issue for preceding element #### Cultural and Linguistic Nuances Report issue for preceding element In order to analyze the presence of cultural and linguistic nuances in our prompts, we create categories of linguistic and cultural nuance using an LLM. Then, we label each prompt in our dataset with its associated nuances. The results of the most common linguistic and cultural phenomena present in the dataset are shown in Table [9](https://arxiv.org/html/2507.17476v1#A1.T9 "Table 9 ‣ Machine Translation and English Reasoning ‣ A.2 Additional Evaluation Results ‣ Annexe A Appendix ‣ MultiNRC: A Challenging and Native Multilingual Reasoning Evaluation Benchmark for LLMs"). The categories of Puns, Homophones, & Wordplay are very common as this includes all examples in the Wordplay category as well as many under Linguistic reasoning. Similarly, Calendar & Time Systems are often present in Math as well as Cultural/Traditions reasoning problems. Report issue for preceding element ### A.2 Additional Evaluation Results Report issue for preceding element #### Language Consistency and Gaps Report issue for preceding element As in Hupkes & Bogoychev ( [2025](https://arxiv.org/html/2507.17476v1#bib.bib15 "")), we show the Mother Tongue Effect, calculated as the average performance in the original language minus the average performance in English over all questions. However, in contrast to Hupkes & Bogoychev ( [2025](https://arxiv.org/html/2507.17476v1#bib.bib15 "")), here we note a negative effect on linguistically and culturally nuanced reasoning questions. We also include model consistency, as a measure of the percentage of questions that a model answers correctly in either original or En divided by the number of questions the model answers correctly in total. For most models, the consistency is around or below 50%, but we note that the top-performing models also have higher consistency, and that consistency has a strong rank correlation with original. The GAP column quantifies this difference between the best-performing language and the worst for each model, with an average gap of 13.90 points across all models. We observed that some models show especially large differences across languages; for example, Deepseek-R1-0528 scores 22.81 points higher in Chinese than in Spanish, and the original Deepseek-R1 a 29.10 difference. This underscores that even strong multilingual models perform very differently across languages. Report issue for preceding element #### Original vs En Examples Report issue for preceding element We provide two examples where o3-2025-04-16-high incorrectly answers the question in French while correctly responding to the English translation in Table [11](https://arxiv.org/html/2507.17476v1#A1.T11 "Table 11 ‣ Machine Translation and English Reasoning ‣ A.2 Additional Evaluation Results ‣ Annexe A Appendix ‣ MultiNRC: A Challenging and Native Multilingual Reasoning Evaluation Benchmark for LLMs"). In the first example, o3 misinterprets the value of a coin in French but correctly identifies it and computes and resulting answer in English. In the second example, a riddle about the color of a sash, o3 incorrectly determines the color sequence and predicts the wrong gender, while in English the model correctly understands the intended colors and predicts the right answer. These cases illustrate how the model may better surface and reason over certain cultural information in English, leading to improved performance. Report issue for preceding element #### Machine Translation and English Reasoning Report issue for preceding element When comparing the reasoning settings in Table [12](https://arxiv.org/html/2507.17476v1#A1.T12 "Table 12 ‣ Machine Translation and English Reasoning ‣ A.2 Additional Evaluation Results ‣ Annexe A Appendix ‣ MultiNRC: A Challenging and Native Multilingual Reasoning Evaluation Benchmark for LLMs"), we find a slight improvement with EnR on average, but this effect varies depending on the model. Furthermore, EnT/R does not offer an improvement on average. The combination of translation error due to native prompt misunderstanding likely contributes to error propagation. We show the delta between Original and En/R according to categories and languages in Table [13](https://arxiv.org/html/2507.17476v1#A1.T13 "Table 13 ‣ Machine Translation and English Reasoning ‣ A.2 Additional Evaluation Results ‣ Annexe A Appendix ‣ MultiNRC: A Challenging and Native Multilingual Reasoning Evaluation Benchmark for LLMs"). Report issue for preceding element We note some improvement from reasoning in English for Chinese prompts, with Math, Linguistic, and Wordplay categories showing average deltas above +1.7. However, we see no improvements in the Cultural category. Even within a particular model, the benefit of reasoning in English often varies depending on both category and language. These results highlight the inherent differences in model families and the heterogenous impact of translation and English reasoning, reinforcing the need for language-specific and model-specific analysis in multilingual benchmarks. . # AraTable: Benchmarking LLMs’ Reasoning and Understanding of Arabic Tabular Data

###### Abstract\
\
Report issue for preceding element\
\
The cognitive and reasoning abilities of large language models (LLMs) have enabled remarkable progress in natural language processing. However, their performance in interpreting structured data, especially in tabular formats, remains limited. Although benchmarks for English tabular data are widely available, Arabic is still underrepresented because of the limited availability of public resources and its unique language features. To address this gap, we present AraTable, a novel and comprehensive benchmark designed to evaluate the reasoning and understanding capabilities of LLMs when applied to Arabic tabular data. AraTable consists of various evaluation tasks, such as direct question answering, fact verification, and complex reasoning, involving a wide range of Arabic tabular sources. Our methodology follows a hybrid pipeline, where initial content is generated by LLMs and subsequently filtered and verified by human experts to ensure high dataset quality. Initial analyses using AraTable show that, while LLMs perform adequately on simpler tabular tasks such as direct question answering, they continue to face significant cognitive challenges when tasks require deeper reasoning and fact verification. This indicates that there are substantial opportunities for future work to improve performance on complex tabular reasoning tasks. We also propose a fully automated evaluation framework that uses a self-deliberation mechanism and achieves performance nearly identical to that of human judges. This research provides a valuable, publicly available resource and evaluation framework that can help accelerate the development of foundational models for processing and analysing Arabic structured data.\

## 1 Introduction\
\
Report issue for preceding element\
\
Large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated remarkable capabilities across a wide range of natural language processing (NLP) tasks, achieving state-of-the-art performance in areas such as text generation \[ [1](https://arxiv.org/html/2507.18442v1#bib.bib1 ""), [2](https://arxiv.org/html/2507.18442v1#bib.bib2 "")\], translation \[ [3](https://arxiv.org/html/2507.18442v1#bib.bib3 ""), [4](https://arxiv.org/html/2507.18442v1#bib.bib4 "")\], and question answering \[ [5](https://arxiv.org/html/2507.18442v1#bib.bib5 ""), [6](https://arxiv.org/html/2507.18442v1#bib.bib6 "")\]. Their ability to process and understand complex textual information has opened up new avenues for the automation and enhancement of various data-driven applications. However, the performance of LLMs is heavily reliant on the nature and structure of the input data. While significant progress has been made in handling unstructured text, evaluating and improving LLM performance on structured data, particularly tabular data, remains a critical area of research.\
\
Report issue for preceding element\
\
Tabular data is widely used in various domains, including finance, healthcare, and public administration, and contains valuable information, organised in rows and columns \[ [7](https://arxiv.org/html/2507.18442v1#bib.bib7 "")\]. Extracting insights and answering questions from tabular data requires models to understand not only the natural language query but also the table structure, the relationships between columns and rows, and the specific values within individual cells. Evaluating LLMs’ performance on tasks involving tabular data, such as question answering based on the information presented in tables, fact verification against tables, and complex reasoning based on tabular information, presents unique challenges \[ [8](https://arxiv.org/html/2507.18442v1#bib.bib8 ""), [9](https://arxiv.org/html/2507.18442v1#bib.bib9 ""), [10](https://arxiv.org/html/2507.18442v1#bib.bib10 "")\]. These tasks require capabilities beyond simple text comprehension, including symbolic reasoning, data aggregation, comparison, mathematical calculation, and logical deduction based on structured facts.\
\
Report issue for preceding element\
\
Although there are general benchmarks for evaluating LLMs’ performance on various tasks, with some recent focus on tabular data in English, such as TableBench \[ [11](https://arxiv.org/html/2507.18442v1#bib.bib11 "")\], DataBench \[ [12](https://arxiv.org/html/2507.18442v1#bib.bib12 "")\], and more recently, MMTU \[ [13](https://arxiv.org/html/2507.18442v1#bib.bib13 "")\], there is a significant gap in comprehensive benchmarks specifically designed to evaluate LLMs’ performance on Arabic tabular data. The Arabic language presents its own set of linguistic complexities, including rich morphology, various dialects, and complex grammar, which can impact an LLM’s ability to process and understand Arabic text, and, consequently, Arabic tabular data. Existing Arabic LLM evaluation efforts, such as the Open Arabic LLM Leaderboard111 [https://huggingface.co/OALL](https://huggingface.co/OALL ""), often focus on general language understanding, with limited attention paid to the challenges of handling structured Arabic information.\
\
Report issue for preceding element\
\
To address this critical gap, this study introduces AraTable, a novel benchmark specifically designed to evaluate the performance of LLMs on Arabic tabular data. This benchmark focuses on three key tasks: direct question answering, fact verification, and reasoning, covering a range of complexity levels and requiring different types of interaction with the tabular structure and content. We considered diverse datasets of Arabic tables from various sources, including Wikipedia, real-world data, and LLM-generated data. Through a comprehensive analysis using AraTable, we evaluated the performance of several prominent LLMs, specifically Llama 3.3 70B \[ [14](https://arxiv.org/html/2507.18442v1#bib.bib14 "")\], Mistral Large\[ [15](https://arxiv.org/html/2507.18442v1#bib.bib15 "")\], DeepSeek-V3\[ [16](https://arxiv.org/html/2507.18442v1#bib.bib16 "")\], and Jais 70B \[ [17](https://arxiv.org/html/2507.18442v1#bib.bib17 "")\]. Across all datasets, our evaluation shows that DeepSeek-V3 consistently outperformed other models, closely followed by Llama 3.3 70B and Mistral Large, while Jais models showed significantly lower accuracy. Direct question-answer (QA) tasks were consistently easier for all models, highlighting a clear gap in performance for more complex reasoning questions, where accuracy often remained below 60%. This indicates a fundamental limitation in current LLMs’ ability to perform complex logical inferences over Arabic tabular data, and that the pure Arabic models, as seen with Jais, are insufficient for complex tabular reasoning.\
\
Report issue for preceding element\
\
Additionally, we introduce and validate a robust evaluation framework specifically designed to assess LLMs’ free text answers and compare them with ground-truth answers. As illustrated in Figure [2](https://arxiv.org/html/2507.18442v1#S5.F2 "Figure 2 ‣ 5 Evaluation ‣ 4.2 Zero-Shot In-Context Learning ‣ 4 Experimental Setting ‣ 3.5 Dataset Statistics ‣ 3.4 Manual Filtering and Verification ‣ 3.3 QA Generation ‣ 3.2 Table Pre-processing ‣ 3.1 Tabular Data Collection ‣ 3 AraTable: Benchmarking LLMs on Arabic Tabular Data ‣ AraTable: Benchmarking LLMs’ Reasoning and Understanding of Arabic Tabular Data"), we first considered a multi-round human evaluation to ensure robustness. Then, we proposed an assisted self-deliberation (ASD) mechanism for LLM-based automatic evaluation. The goal is to provide a reliable, unbiased, automatic evaluation process of the models’ answers for AraTable benchmarking that closely aligns with human judgement.\
\
Report issue for preceding element\
\
This work provides a valuable resource for the research community, enabling more targeted development and evaluation of LLMs for Arabic tabular data processing and contributing to the advancement of Arabic natural language understanding in the structured domains. The main contributions of this study can be summarised as follows:\
