# D. Case Study\
\
Figure 5 illustrates a pair of practical examples for GPT-3.5- Turbo on bilingual programming tasks. In the first example in Figure 5(a), GPT-3.5-Turbo generates the correct code for the Chinese input but fails to do so for the English input. Specifically, the solution “return total//n” (marked in red) does not align with the task description of returning the result ”in a rounded integer.” This further emphasizes the need for an interpretability-driven comprehensive study regarding which key entities or information from input problems are captured by LCGMs for different input languages.\
\
Moreover, we find that even when LCGMs generate functionally correct code for both English and Chinese inputs, there can still be significant differences in the efficiency of the generated code. As shown in the second example in Figure 5(b), the code generated for the Chinese input is less efficient than that for the English input. The average execution time complexity of the code generated for the Chinese input is $O ( n ^ { 2 } )$ due to the presence of nested loops. In contrast, the code generated for the English input has an average time complexity of only $O ( n \* \\log ( n ) )$ , thanks to the more concise and efficient library call of “sort()”. This may inspire us that the subjective enthusiasm of LCGMs for library API calls may affect the overall efficiency of their generated code. It is worth noting that to better control variables and ensure that the Chinese-English differences in the input exist only in the programming question descriptions, we used the same English prompt for code generation in both languages.\
\
# E. Discussions and Suggections\
\
Comprehensive Multilingual Code Generation Quality Assessment: Based on the results from RQ1 and RQ2, our study has revealed significant disparities in the effectiveness and efficiency of LCGMs in generating code for bilingual (Chinese and English) programming. It is reasonable to infer that such differences are not confined to these two languages but may represent a broader phenomenon. Emerging research has increasingly investigated the multilingual understanding and generation capabilities of Large Language Models \[30\], and similar scrutiny must be directed towards LCGMs. Moreover, effectiveness and efficiency are only two aspects of code quality, other important attributes such as security, readability, and maintainability also deserve consideration. Therefore, expanding the scope of quality assessment to include these additional attributes is a valuable direction for future research. Developing Better Prompting Methods. According to RQ3, the impact of different prompting strategies on the quality of LCGM-generated code is substantial. Prompting techniques are pivotal in the era of LLMs, and well-crafted prompts can significantly enhance the quality of generation \[31\]. Investigating how to construct superior prompts that enable LCGMs to consistently produce high-quality code across different languages is of paramount importance.\
\
Adaptive Temperature Tuning. It has been observed that as the temperature parameter increases, LCGMs exhibit varying performance across languages, i.e., most LCGMs tend to prefer generating code of higher quality in English. Identifying the optimal temperature settings that allow LCGMs to perform best for each language could be a key factor in improving multilingual code generation.\
\
In summary, one important message from this study is that the software engineering community should establish benchmarks and frameworks for evaluating the multilingual code generation capabilities of LCGMs, considering different code quality assessment metrics, input languages, prompting methods, and more. As an initial step, we have released our framework \[12\] and strongly encourage our readers to contribute more datasets and code quality measurements.\
\
# F. Threats to Validity\
\
Limited Dataset: The dataset utilized in this study, despite careful designing, is limited to 52 bilingual programming questions, which may not sufficiently cover the diverse range of tasks LCGMs encounter in practical applications. Furthermore, the dataset only includes English and Chinese, potentially failing to capture the performance variations of LCGMs across a wider array of languages. This limitation stems from the requirement of strong language proficiency to ensure the quality of multilingual parallel data.\
\
Limited LCGMs: The selected six LCGMs represent the current technology but don’t cover all models or training methods. However, the selected LCGMs serve as the foundation for many advanced LCGMs. Our evaluation method is universal and extendable to a broader range of models.\
\
Evaluation Metrics: The metrics employed in this study primarily focus on code correctness and efficiency, potentially neglecting other crucial aspects of code quality, such as readability, maintainability, and adherence to coding standards. The absence of these factors in the evaluation process may restrict the comprehensive understanding of the LCGM’ performance.\
\
To mitigate the threats and foster further research, we make our collected dataset and evaluation framework publicly available \[12\]. This initiative aims to empower researchers to expand the study by incorporating diverse programming tasks, languages, and quality assessment metrics, as well as to include a broader range of LCGMs in the comparison.\
\
# V. RELATED WORK\
\
# A. Large Code Generation Models\
\
LLMs have achieved impressive results in code processing, with models ranging from general-purpose to specialized architectures. General-purpose LLMs, such as LLaMA \[32\], Llama2 \[33\], LaMDA \[34\], and PaLM \[35\], can generate code thanks to pre-training on text data that includes code. For example, Llama2 contains 328GB of code from GitHub. Even smaller models like Phi-1.5 (1.3 billion parameters) can demonstrate coding proficiency \[36\].\
\
Language models with additional pre-training on code have achieved new benchmarks. Codex \[8\] fine-tuned GPT-3 on 100B code tokens, and PaLM-Coder \[35\] extended pretraining with 7.8 billion tokens of code. CodeLlama \[25\] enhanced Llama2 by pre-training it on 500 billion code tokens, and CodeFuse-CodeLlama \[37\], a fine-tuned version of CodeLlama, surpasses even GPT-4’s performance.\
\
Specialized architecture models use different architectures to generate code. CodeT $^ { 5 + }$ \[38\] uses an encoder-decoder architecture with contrastive objectives, while CodeFusion \[39\] introduces diffusion models to code modeling. These models can outperform other LLMs on code synthesis datasets.\
\
# B. Testing and Evaluation for Code Generation Model\
\
Over the years, the software engineering community has proposed various evaluation tasks to assess code models, which have been consolidated into benchmarks such as CodeXGLUE \[40\] and CodeBLEU \[41\]. However, with the introduction of HumanEval \[8\] and the increasing capability of code generation models, the focus has shifted towards functional correctness as a more appropriate metric for evaluation \[42\], \[43\], \[9\]. This has led to the development of metrics such as $\\operatorname { p a s s } @ \\operatorname { k }$ \[8\] and passn $@ \\mathbf { k }$ \[44\], which assess the model’s ability to generate code that passes unit tests. Several benchmarks have been created to evaluate code synthesis, including HUMANEVAL and MBPP \[9\] for Python, as well as benchmarks targeting other programming languages such as SQL (Spider\[45\]), $\\mathrm { C } { + + }$ , JavaScript, and Go (HUMANEVALX \[24\]), $\\mathrm { C } { + } { + }$ and Java (CodeContests \[44\]), and a multilingual extension of HUMANEVAL and MBPP (MultiPL-E \[46\]). In addition to function-level evaluation, CrossCodeEval \[47\] and CoderEval \[48\] have introduced benchmarks for crossfile and project-level code completion. Besides correctness evaluation, some works are dedicated to testing and assessing the robustness of LCGMs \[49\], \[50\], \[51\], \[52\], \[53\].\
\
# VI. CONCLUSION\
\
In this paper, we conduct a pioneering empirical study on the bilingual code generation quality of Large Code Generation Models (LCGMs). While LCGMs have revolutionized software engineering tasks such as code generation, their performance on non-English languages, particularly Chinese, has not been systematically investigated. We collect a dataset containing 52 bilingual parallel programming tasks and evaluate the code generated by six state-of-the-art LCGMs in terms of effectiveness and efficiency. Our findings reveal that there exist quality differences between LCGM-generated code for English and Chinese programming questions. This work underscores the urgency for further research and development to ensure consistent code generation across languages.\
